speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider abolishing the regional rates of pay, now in force for certain federal government employees, in accordance with its stated policy of pay equity.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pride that I rise once again to speak in this House about the issue of regional rates of pay. Some people might remember, I think it was June last year, when I had the pleasure of rising in this place to address a similar motion concerning this foreign practice.
I looked at Hansard from June of last year, when this motion was up in the last session for debate. I noticed that there was a consistency in the approach by members opposite on the government side and that they did not want to speak to the issue of regional rates of pay. They wanted to play semantics dealing with whether or not this was a pay equity issue. They spent a considerable period of time missing the issue.
Before we start today I would like to say, right off the bat, what I believe this is all about. The lack of national rates of pay in some categories within the federal Public Service means that we do not truly have pay equity. What pay equity means is equal pay for work of equal value.
It is the stated belief of the government, and governments across this country, that people should be paid for the effort and skill they put into their work, not based on the colour of their skin, their gender, and certainly not on their language. It appears that there is an anomaly in
this one situation because this government continues to support a system of regional rates of pay.
Quite simply what that means is that a pipefitter in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia gets paid considerably less working for the Government of Canada doing a contract job as described by the government than an individual in any of a number of regions as defined by the government. In particular, they get paid about $6 an hour less in some circumstances than those people doing the same job, with the same skills, for the same government in other places, particularly on the west coast.
We have to look at the history of this. The government is going to get up and tell us that regional rates of pay have been there for a long period of time. At one time there were 30 or 40 different regional rates. That is what they are going to tell us.
Then they will come back and say that they are working toward that and there are only 10 or 12 regions left whereby by legislation we discriminate against individuals.
I want to make something very clear. Wage discrimination that is based on where a person lives is no less abhorrent than wage discrimination based on gender, language, or skin colour. There is no difference. Maybe what we have to do down on the east coast-and I say it tongue-in-cheek; perhaps the government is simply not moved by the argument-is speak some type of pig Latin or perhaps adopt Gaelic as our language in places like Nova Scotia. Then we could go to the Human Rights Commission and get an order that says to this government that it cannot discriminate against this particular group of workers. It cannot pay workers less on the east coast than it does in other parts of the country.
In the dark old days it was acceptable to do that, but the country has changed. Tomorrow proposals will be tabled in this House in an effort to try to keep this country together. What we always hear in proposals that come forward to rebuild a country is that we must, through our Constitution and through our legislation, inject equity and fairness to all Canadians. It is interesting to note that when this motion was debated by me the last time, we were in the midst of the road running between the Chateau Laurier and the Congress Centre. It was a year ago June, when Meech Lake was just about

September 23, 1991
Private Members' Business
to hit the rocks. I noted then with some irony that the first ministers of this country were down the road talking about drafting a document to instil fairness and equality, but their members were standing up in this House and saying no to pay equity in regional rates of pay.
I want to list a couple of groups, and I will do this rather quickly because I have a lot to say on this issue. There are a number of groups that are paid, not according to the job they do or the quality of their skills but by where they work. They are all employed by the federal government. Scientific and professional category, education, seven different regional rates; nursing, eight different regional rates; occupational physical therapy, seven different regional rates. The list goes on. Occupational categories, I am going to spend most of my time dealing with this. General labour and trade-ten different zones.
It means that a pipefitter or a sheet metal worker can get any one of ten different rates of pay. I can guarantee that in almost every single case a pipefitter in Atlantic Canada is going to get the lowest rate of pay. That is what regional rates of pay have done to us.
Way down at the bottom is ship repair. There are only two rates, east and west. The Halifax-Dartmouth shipyards, the government shipyards, are the ones that the Prime Minister during the Persian Gulf situation got up and applauded in this House for the incredible effort that they put into refitting the vessels that we were sending over into a theatre of war. He said what marvellous men and women they were and they rose to the call of duty. It doesn't sound like the type of individuals to me that are so bloody greedy that they are absolutely intent on screwing the government out of a few dollars in the interests of fairness and equity. But yet those same dockyard workers down in Halifax-Dartmouth, over 1,200 of them, are currently without pay equity.
I want to refer to a paper here. I met with the unions and I talked to them and said: "Look, you know regional rates of pay are going to go by way of the dinosaur, but we have got to push on it". But I look here and see on a wage scale chart that the same workers, federal government dockyard workers on the west coast, in May 1990 were paid an average 14 per cent higher than those on the east coast. By January 1991-and keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the government says it is trying to collapse these regional rates-the discrepancy rose to 19 per cent. In October 1992 it will be up to 28.35 per cent difference, and yet the government gets up and talks about its absolute commitment to pay equity. Absolute hogwash, Mr. Speaker.
A couple of interesting things have happened. Back in the fall of 1989 we had a situation arise where the ships' crews, normally designated as essential employees so that they cannot go out on strike, were without a contract for a significant period of time. These men and women who worked on ships' crews on the east and west coast, mostly on the east coast, made a decision that enough was enough. They were no longer going to sit back and be loyal little lap dogs to the government and accept significantly lower salaries for a dangerous job that they did on behalf of the Canadian government and the Canadian public.
They went out on strike. It was not because they were looking for massive increases. The government opposite had painted these employees as greedy. Do you know how much they got paid, Mr. Speaker? The average pay for a ship's crew employee on the east coast of Canada was between $19,000 and $22,000 a year. Boy, they had cushy jobs, too, you know: all they had to do was risk their lives for the people of Canada! They were on Coast Guard vessels and when there was a storm and there was a ship in trouble, they went out on the high seas and risked their lives for $19,000 or $21,000 a year. But this government, as callous as it is, was then and continues to be, absolutely refused the one small request to pay the people on the east coast who risked their lives for this country and this government the same as the people on the west coast.
They forced them out on strike and we saw this awful legislation introduced in the House, strike breaking legislation, to force them back to work. The Liberals and the New Democrats opposite held that legislation up, and we forced the government every step of the way to invoke closure every step of the way.
September 23, 1991

When it was all over and done with, my colleague here from Ottawa, who is a Public Service critic, filibustered in this House to ensure that the rights of those workers, the ships' crews and other public servants were not going to be trampled on easily in this place.
So what happened? They went to arbitration. The government refused to close a wage rate between the east and west coasts, perhaps causing a problem with public safety. At least it claimed it at the time, although we objected and said that was not the case.
What happened when it went to arbitration? I want the members opposite to listen. The government refuses to negotiate in good faith when it is dealing with regional rates of pay or with any public servant, as we saw with the recent PSAC strike.
The binding arbitration report, after this government legislated those $19,000 to $21,000 a year employees back to work, said clearly that effective the date of the signing of this collective agreement the following would happen: (a) it would bring east coast rates of pay to parity with the west coast rates of pay.
It is clear. A three-party arbitration panel with a member of the government could not even justify the further discriminatory practice of allowing regional rates of pay. It was an unnecessary strike it forced those workers out on, because it really does not care.
There is another thing that is interesting if you look at the guidelines, and I want to read this one: "Federal Public Service compensation policy-guiding principles". These are pretty interesting. It says that the employer's approach to compensation determination for federal public servants shall follow some guidelines: (a) that public sector compensation be fair to employees and to the tax paying public. We hear them twist that one around all the time and say that the poorest of the poor are not worthy of a decent liveable wage-we heard that last week when we had the strike-and (b) that public sector compensation be related in a reasonable and acceptable way to the private sector, with compensation not exceeding that paid for similar services by the private sector.
I want to highlight that because when this motion was put last June all we heard from the members opposite reading by line from a speech prepared by Treasury
Private Members' Business
Board was that they cannot do away with regional rates of pay because if they did, the private sector in those areas would collapse as the rates of pay would be too high.
One cannot have it both ways. I want to go back to the ships' crews strike. It is pretty interesting. The government refused to admit that the binding arbitration was found to be factual. In dealing with the ships' crews strike it says when the government refused to pay them a living wage: "We are also satisfied in the peculiar circumstances of this case that there is legitimacy to the alliance claim that a significant and glaring disparity has developed over the past several rounds of negotiations with respect to the compensation paid to government ships' crews as compared to ships' crews in the private sector".
It goes further somewhere else in the decision to say that if allowed to go unchecked it would reach 38 per cent disparity. The government wants to claim that it cannot touch these regional rates because somehow it is going to have a massive negative impact on the private sector. Hogwash. Nonsense. This government continues to perpetuate a policy that should have died in the dark ages of wage discrimination based on where an individual lives.
Back over to the dock workers, 1,230 or 1,240 souls, the same people who fitted up in record time the Canadian navy in its valiant effort with the UN in the Persian Gulf. Those individuals are now negotiating a contract again. The charge hands who were sort of the supervisory personnel went straight to binding arbitration. I do not have a copy of the report with me, but my understanding is that that binding arbitration when it came down a week ago Friday clearly and up front said that the regional rate of pay had to be collapsed and that a national rate of pay had to be instituted.
It is not just me standing here telling this House of Commons that this motion should be acceptable and that the government should look at it. The government's own process of arbitration in dealing with many of these groups that are affected, particularly on the Atlantic Coast, in a very negative way by the discriminatory practice of regional rates of pay, of paying somebody less for a job based on where they live, has gone the way of the dodo bird.
September 23, 1991

Private Members' Business
It has got to go. Maybe the message, if the government did not have before us some Draconian legislation, could basically destroy the collective bargaining process. All of those groups affected by regional rates of pay should simply say: "We want binding arbitration".
The record since a year is clear. In each and every case where regional rates of pay were an issue and went to binding arbitration, the panel said: "Enough of this. We have to close that wage gap". That is exactly what we have to do.
There are a couple of other issues here that have to be addressed. One is whether this government is truly concerned about fairness and equity. I did not have a chance in the short debate that we had on the awful back-to-work legislation this government put forward to challenge or question the government's credibility when it talks about its wish to have pay equity.
It wants to look at pay equity as a gender problem within the federal Public Service. It talks about how it wants to get rid of discriminatory practices and what wonderful people it thinks our public servants are.
I will read a couple of quotes by our own Prime Minister. I think they clearly indicated the disdain and the disgust with which this government treats public servants, most of all those public servants who do a damn good job for this country for very little remuneration and very little credit from the current government.
As reported in The Ottawa Citizen, April 9, 1983: "Any bureaucrat who did try to oppose him (Mulroney) would be greeted with the words 'Voila ton pink slip'".
Another interesting quote from our Prime Minister, the head of our government which espouses that it truly believes in and is in pursuit of wage parity, "pay equity", is from CBOT, Newsday, May 26, 1983. Talking about the Public Service, he said: "They have never worked a day in their lives. They have never done a day's work". That sort of says it all.
This government under the leadership of this Prime Minister is absolutely intent. It always has to have an enemy, and the enemy that it has chosen in the last number of years is the federal Public Service.
One of many.

One of many.
In conclusion, I would urge the government, if it does not want to listen to me, to look at its arbitration reports. Will the government for once do the right thing and agree that in 1991 there is no place in a modem democracy for a system of pay by the federal government, the people who legislate laws in this country and pass laws and codes of behaviour by statute, which is abhorrent and discriminatory, a rate of pay which does not pay individuals for the work they put into products but rather pays them according to where they live in this country.
I would hope, now that it is the second time around on this particular motion, that the government would look at the record and see fit to announce forthwith through President of the Treasury Board, in spite of the regressive freeze legislation that it has on, that regional rates of pay are going to be exempt from that and that the gap will be closed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this issue as the member has said is on its second trip around the racetrack. It was featured during the 1988 election, particularly in Halifax.
It has been the policy of various governments since 1967 and continues to be the policy of the government today to reflect local rates of pay for Public Service employees in occupations where outside data indicate significant variations from the national average.
In other words, we tend to reflect the regional rates in the wages that we pay for the various jobs. It is not just ships' crews and repair crews and so forth. It covers a whole range of public servants in various regions of the country. We cannot say that it just covers two groups, because that would be another case to be made.
My remarks are somewhat constrained, but I do note that a small group of employees in the Saskatoon area is challenging the regional rate policy of the government under section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Since the court proceedings have commenced on this issue, it would not appropriate to get into anything more than generalities and general comments on this issue.
In his comments the member mentioned and equated regional rates with equal pay for work of equal value. He knows full well that the government has passed legislation pertaining to equal pay for work of equal value. He
September 23, 1991

knows also that there have been considerable payments and adjustments made as the result of that legislation.
I am just looking for the bill here. I think it was June 1986 that the bill was passed. The member should recall the comments of the President of the Treasury Board of the day in January 1990 regarding equal pay for work of equal value. He announced that the first phase of lump sum payments would be $317 million and it would be made as quickly as possible. This is a gender difference in wage rates, where men and women are doing essentially the same work. The feeling is and the government policy is that they should be paid the same rate.
In the announcement that the President of the Treasury Board made on January 26, 1990 he said that the rates would be retroactive to March 1,1985. The retroactive payment will average something like $4,800 per employee affected. The affected employees work in all parts of Canada and therefore it is not reasonable in that sense.
The second phase involves $76 million in annual salary adjustments effective April 1, 1990. The amount of wage adjustments and retroactive payments will vary depending on the pay disparity identified for any particular occupational group and the amount of time an employee has been in a particular position or positions.
We have moved substantially on pay equity. My secretary was telling me the other day about a young lady who worked on the Hill, then left the Hill to work in another government department and has now returned to the Hill. To her surprise she received a cheque in the amount of something like $3,700. When she inquired as to what it was for, she was told that it was pay equity. It is going on and it is working.
This matter of regional rates is a difficult one. Living conditions vary from one part of the country to another. I do not suppose there is a trade category that could be imagined, whether it is auto mechanics, plumbing or any craft or trade in which the rates are uniform across the country. They are not uniform across the country. They are not uniform in the private sector across the country.
Private Members' Business
The concern, not only of this government but of previous governments, has always been: Are we going to distort the local situation? Are we going to cause a distortion in the private sector if we pay a rate in Halifax that is paid in Vancouver?
The other thing the member is missing in his comments are the fringe benefits. There is no regional disparity in fringe benefits whatever, and he knows that. He should reflect on that as well. There are substantial fringe benefits and they are all subject to negotiations. I do not suppose there has been a negotiation between the Public Service unions and the government in the last many years that has not had this issue of regional rates as part of the discussion. I have no doubt in my mind that the discussions going on this very day, probably this very hour, between the President of the Treasury Board and Daryl Bean and the PSAC negotiators have the regional rates on the table and are being discussed.
Since we have been in government, since 1984, we have followed the practice established in 1967. That is not to justify it in any way, but that is the practice and that is what it has always been. I believe the concern is that in an area where there may not be absolute boom conditions and tradesmen are not paid substantially higher wages than Public Service employees, if we moved to raise those rates beyond the local rate that is being paid, we would cause some very serious economic conditions within that area.
The other point that the member has not talked about is skills. These rates are based on base rates, but there are skills rates beyond that which he has not dealt with. Many of those persons, by updating their skills, could have an increase in their wages.
First of all, I reject the comparison of pay of equal value to regional rates. I just do not think it is a valid comparison.
As I said, the matter is before the court in Saskatoon and we will have to see where that plays out but, at the present time, that is where the policy of the government lies and we will reflect local rates in our regional rate efforts.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of the motion put to the House by the member for Dartmouth.

Private Members' Business
Primarily what this motion does is try to bring together the outlying areas of our country to the central part of our country. We are trying to bring people together.
What I hear from the government side is that we are going to cause an imbalance by agreeing to this motion. We are going to cause an imbalance in the area that we are servicing. The private sector will not be able to afford to keep up with the rates of pay.
The member from the government side just indicated that the government has already introduced pay equity for gender reasons and it has sent cheques out to various regions. I did not hear him saying that it has caused problems in the private sector. It brought them together.
When we look at the trades and we talk about skills, if I were a tradesman on either coast or anywhere in this country, I would take personal offence at the comment that was made by the member opposite when he said that skills enter the picture. I was a plumber before I became a politician and I am as much a plumber on the west coast as I am on the east coast as I am in Ontario. My skills do not vary. Why is there a difference in the rates of pay for shipbuilders, for pipefitters, for electricians and for other trades? A buck is a buck and a pipefitter is a pipefitter.
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think what this government is trying to do is to create, with these regional rates, dissension within the ranks and keep them arguing between each other so that they can pit one against the other and have them say: "I am better than you are because I am getting paid more." I think we all have something to offer. I think we are entitled to equal pay for work of equal value. To tell someone that their work is not as valuable as someone else's is a severe slap in the fact to that individual.
We cannot continue to have these regional rates of pay because we are classifying when we do that. No one in this House or in this country is any better than anyone else and is no worse than anyone else.
I would like all members in this House to ask themselves this question. Would they consider taking less pay as members of Parliament because they come from different regions of this country? I think the answer is quite clear. We all figure we are doing as good a job as the other person and we want to get the same amount of money as that person. That is no more or no less than any other government employee is asking for.
I think my comments are relatively brief but to the point. I think that we need to have a national rate of pay for all our government employees. They contribute as much as anyone else in this country and they do not deserve to be treated any less or any differently than anyone else. I certainly hope that the Conservative members will come to their senses and support this very important and very needed motion.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this motion by the hon. member for Dartmouth. The hon. member for Dartmouth has been pushing this issue ever since he became a member of Parliament.
Coming from Newfoundland, I appreciate having a fellow member pushing the issue as hard as he has pushed it. I have watched him in caucus as well make the same points over and over and over again. I think that the message is getting through.
If you are a machine operator with the same employer, working in Saskatchewan, you can go up to $15 an hour. But if you are working in British Columbia, excluding metropolitan Vancouver and metropolitan Victoria, you can go up to $18.84 an hour, a difference of almost $4 an hour. If you are an electrician, you can go to the top of your scale to $16.31 if you work in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island, $16.31, but if you were in metropolitan Vancouver, metropolitan Victoria, you could go up to $20.71 an hour. That is a difference of $4 an hour.
Some occupations have a difference of $5 an hour. Some of them are $6 an hour, doing the same job with the same employer. It depends on where you are working. These are all tradesmen, receiving $3 or $4 an hour difference, depending on where they are working.
The federal government, as the member for Dartmouth knows, keeps coming back as the representative of the government said a few moments ago, and saying: "We want to keep it down to the going rates in the area so that it will not be an unfair competition with the private sector in that area". That argument fails and it fails badly because of a couple of points. Number one, the federal government turns around in some of those same areas where the wages are being paid are low because of the going rates, says the government, and gives them environmental allowances on top of the wage or gives them isolation pay on top of the wage. There is no logic behind where the dividing line is, Mr. Speaker. I cite you an example. A few moments ago the hon. member representing the New Democratic Party said that he was a plumber before becoming a member of Parliament. If he were a plumber in British Columbia working for the federal government, excluding metropol-
September 23, 1991

itan Vancouver he would start at $17.11 an hour. But, if he were working in metropolitan Vancouver, he would be making $17.69 an hour. In other words, if he were working in metropolitan Vancouver he would make more than if he were working in B.C. outside metropolitan Vancouver as a plumber. If he was a pipefitter he would make $12.09 an hour if he was in British Columbia excluding metropolitan Vancouver, he would make less than that, $11.92, if he were in metropolitan Vancouver.
It makes no sense.

Here we go. We have a plumber who is paid more if he is in metropolitan Vancouver than if he is outside and we have pipefitter who is paid less if he is in metropolitan Vancouver than if he is outside. It is utter nonsense. It is complete and total nonsense. It is a violation of the human rights of an individual.
Some reference has been made here to the fact that the Human Rights Commission has always turned around on the basis of what is in the Human Rights Act. They cite section 11 of the act, and I don't have to cite section 11 for the hon. member for Dartmouth or for any other member. They know that it says that an employer cannot pay different wages to a male and female if they are working in the same establishment and doing the same work or work of equal value. They say that is not a violation of the Human Rights Act.
I suppose we could say that they are not working in the same establishment. They are working for the same employer and there is a dividing line. It is not only by province, but if one works inside or outside a metropolitan area. However, certainly, the principle of fairness is absent in regional rates of pay.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, a group of federal employees who are sent to a location on a big job, and you have one from this area and another from that area and they are all carpenters, say, and every single one of them is making different wages because they have been sent in from their home territory where they normally work to do a job? Can you imagine how people feel who are mobile in the Public Service, as we had the case a
Private Members' Business
couple of years ago of the crews where they would all meet in Cambridge Bay up in the Northwest Passage? They would tie their boats up, and one fellow was making $3 an hour more than another fellow. The ship repair crews-the hon. member for Dartmouth has 300 or 400 or 500 I suppose in his riding- have different rates depending on where they are from. It just so happens that the hon. member is representing the lower end of the scale. These people are doing the same work, the same job as everybody else is doing.
This has led to a demoralization of the Public Service. The Canadian public expects service from the Public Service; they expect service from them. Here are public servants working in Gander, Newfoundland or in Grand Falls, Newfoundland or Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, and they are doing the same job as somebody living in another province and they are being paid less. They are being paid $7,000 a year less than somebody in the same classification, but they are working in a different area of Canada. It is demoralization of the Public Service.
The Government of Canada is always trying to do things to increase productivity. It paid out big productivity bonuses recently to the fat cats, the big guys making all the money. It paid them these big bonuses, payoffs for layoffs, to get rid of people.
You are always looking over your shoulder wondering who is making judgment on you today. Here you are sitting down doing a job somebody else is doing, same classification, same work, and receiving $4 an hour less because of where you live in this country, with the same employer. Then you have a manager looking down your shoulder and you know that if that manager manages to get rid of you he gets a bonus a Christmastime.
The Government of Canada should not just pay attention to what is in the Canadian Human Rights Act. No act of Parliament is without its mistakes, and there were mistakes made when this legislation was passed. Surely by strict common sense no member of Parliament would like to be paid on the basis of regional rates of pay. Mr. Speaker, on a scale of 12, your province is about number three from the bottom.

September 23, 1991
Private Members' Business
Just imagine if members of Parliament were paid on the basis of regional rates of pay. It would not be a very attractive business for somebody from eastern Canada, I can assure you of that.

Mr. Speaker, the member for Dartmouth, in bringing this matter to the attention of the House of Commons, namely the subject of pay equality across the nation, joins the ranks and choruses of a number of members who have raised this point in the past including myself.
I want to begin by telling all members that I have canvassed this subject from a to z and all aspects of it. So I make the comments I make today on the basis of that study over a period of time.
First of all let me make it clear there is a principle involved which the Canadian Public Service has accepted for decades. That is that public service compensation must be fair to both the employer and the employee and to the taxpayer.
The second aspect of that principle is that public sector compensation should be related in a reasonable and acceptable way to the private sector. We have to keep that as the guiding light. We cannot simply abandon those principles to appease workers in a particular area because, as I have pointed out on occasions in the past, it can have a detrimental effect. The member for Gander-Grand Falls never mentioned this aspect. On whether he knows about it or not I will not comment, but I will take two minutes to explain to the member what happens.
First of all, if you grant rates of pay that are out of context with the private sector in the regional area, you definitely create two kinds of havoc. First you will raise compensation for trades people beyond reasonable levels applicable to that region. You will have every plumber, every electrician, seeking employment in the public sector and leaving jobs in the private sector. The only way the employers in the private sector can compensate is by providing higher wages which increases the prices to consumers, that is the people of Canada, the taxpayers of Canada. They will pay more for services in their region because the Government of Canada has artificially increased compensation in trades and occupations in that area. That is number one detrimental effect that I hope the member for Dartmouth recognizes and realizes, because the member for Gander-Grand Falls apparently does not.
The second point is this: everybody agreed-and I am sure every member of the Liberal Party including their leader, House leader, and officials would agree-that the taxpayer of Canada is entitled to the best deal possible in terms of economies for government services. You have to face the fact that if the government can provide a service at less cost to the taxpayer in a certain way, then the government has some obligation to adopt that way of providing that service.
What does that mean in terms of compensation? That means very simply that if you pay higher rates than are justified in a region, the government will be paying more for the services it is acquiring.
If you pay painters at CFB Halifax more money than painters normally receive in the Halifax-Dartmouth area, you will raise the cost of painting in public buildings, or at least the buildings at CFB Halifax. What is the result of that? Painters in private industry will come to the government and ask: "Why are you paying so much extra to paint buildings in the Halifax-Dartmouth area when we can do it cheaper?" It does not make any difference what parliamentarians say. It does not make any difference what the member from Dartmouth says, because people in the private sector will come to government and say: "Why are you paying $1,000 or $10,000 or $100,000 extra for painting services in the Halifax-Dartmouth area when we can do it for less? We will employ people. We will cause industrial expansion and create local economic benefits and you do not have the right as the government to stop that".
When the member for Dartmouth stands up to defend what he calls pay equality, which means substantial increases in pay for people in his constituency and people in my constituency, I want him to say at the same time and at the same place: "You realize that in doing this we will be paying more taxpayers' money out than we need to pay and it will have a detrimental effect on the private sector". There will be painters, for example, in the private sector unemployed. There will be painting contractors without work because we have taken it upon ourselves to artificially raise levels of pay and to cause that havoc to occur. He has to take both sides of the coin.
September 23, 1991

If I had my choice, I would simply sign an equality of pay order for the whole Public Service and let the chips fall where they may. Why would I do that? Because that is the easiest way out for me. That would make life easier for me. Just give it away. Give the employees what they want. Make them happy. They would be patting me on the back. They would be inviting me to their union meetings. They would be sending me Christmas cards. It would be wonderful.
However that is not my obligation as a representative of the public. My obligation as an elected member of Parliament is to do the right thing, to weigh all the factors and make a decision on the basis of all of those factors.
I have pressed time and time again in this House and in all channels and corridors of government for equal pay with persons on the west coast, and every time I have had my foot caught in a trap. When I stood in this House and other places and asked for equal pay with ships' crews in British Columbia, did they say: "yes, that is fine, thank you very much", when they got equal pay? No.
You can get equal pay simply by equalizing everybody's pay. You can reduce wages on the west coast compared to wages on the east coast and create equality. Does anybody want that? Has any union member ever come forward and said: "Look, we will use the same amount of money but we will equally divide it among us"? No, no, no, that is not the kind of equal pay. They are simply talking about an increase in pay. I understand that. I would like to have an increase in pay. I know they would like to have an increase in pay. Everybody would like to have an increase in pay, but we have to look at the political realities, at the economic realities.
When we raised the pay to equal levels for the ships' crews as the member for Dartmouth well knows-and I think I had a great part in that action-what happened? We simply gave Daryl Bean and the Public Service Alliance of Canada an opportunity to say that everybody should get that increase. The man who said he wanted equality of pay for ships' crews then turned around and said that everybody should get a similar increase right across the Public Service.
That was my sojourn into the area of collective bargaining. I am content to leave it now to Treasury Board officials because after that they reminded me: "See what you did. All you did was discolour the waters

of collective bargaining, of bargaining back and forth, by insisting on wage equality".
If the member for Dartmouth or the member for Gander-Grand Falls wants to step in there and disturb these relations, deal with them politically, not economically, not sensibly, then let it be on his shoulders. Let him ask for increases that are going to cause all kinds of turmoil. Does he think that painters at the dockyard are going to be happy with the increase they get if they reach equality without any effect on painters in other areas of the government, in other areas such as the hospitals which hire hundreds of painters and the private sector? No, it will simply cause a wage escalation.
While we would like to see equality, while we want to see fairness, we can only achieve that through sensible bargaining. The members at CFB Halifax in the ship repair unit know that, because I told them that. I told them that time and time again: "I will do what I can for you. I will advocate your cause, but we are up against a system that was brought into force many years ago by the Liberal government". It is okay for those Liberals on that side and the NDP to say they want pay equality. They not only denied pay equality in the Liberal term of office, but they refused to move toward equality. All I have ever asked them to do, and I told this to the representatives of the dockyard workers union, the ship repair unit, Jim Henneberry and his colleagues, that I would simply ask the government to move towards pay equality, to approach it and to keep it in mind as a goal or an objective to win.
Of course, we fought this all out in the 1988 election. We had parades and demonstrations. I never varied from my position. I told the dockyard workers exactly what my position was and I am telling them again today, for the umpteenth time, that I believe we want to work towards equality but we cannot reach it all in one jump. By the way, they accepted that position on December 6, 1988, when they accepted the pay increase. After rejecting it, they accepted the pay increase.
Jim Henneberry and his colleagues at the dockyard and labour leaders throughout the Public Service realize what is at stake here. They realize what principles are involved. If they can get yet another politician to come forward and say: "We want it now", I do not blame them for doing that. I think in their hearts they know it is something that has to be achieved through a gradual, evolutionary process.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to support the motion put forward by my hon. friend from Dartmouth.
The issue before the House is fairness. During the recent Public Service strike, one of the key union demands was the elimination of regional rates of pay. This is a system that discriminates against people on the basis of where they live.
Something has to be made perfectly clear. The elimination of regional rates of pay is not about equal pay for work of equal value. It is about paying people the same wage for doing exactly the same job for the same boss regardless of where they live. The federal government pays people a different salary depending on whether they live in Montague in my riding or Toronto or a community like Terrace, British Columbia.
The people who suffer the most from this unfair system are the people of Atlantic Canada and of course, the people of my riding of Cardigan, Prince Edward Island. Of the 17 job classes in the general labour and trade section of the federal Public Service, seven groups have their lowest rates of pay in Atlantic Canada.
We are not talking about paying somebody a few cents an hour more because the cost of living is much higher in Toronto. We are talking about paying an electrician in Souris, Prince Edward Island 20 per cent less than an electrician in Revelstoke, British Columbia, who is doing exactly the same job for the same boss but is being paid over $3 an hour less for doing the same job.
People in my riding would like to know where the fairness is in this system. I want to assure members that I have nothing against the people of British Columbia. The people of British Columbia are as honest and hard working as the people of Prince Edward Island.
The electrician in Prince Edward Island works just as hard as his counterpart in British Columbia, yet this government insists on paying the electrician from Souris,
Prince Edward Island, 20 per cent less. This problem not only deals with electricians, but it deals with boilermakers, tool and die operators, farm hands, plumbers, mechanics, carpenters and others, all who suffer from this discriminatory policy of the federal government.
I am not suggesting that the people in Toronto or Revelstoke should take a cut in pay and be brought down to the level of the people in Atlantic Canada or, in fact, the people of Saskatchewan who suffer the same discriminatory practices. Rather, I suggest that the people of Atlantic Canada, Saskatchewan and other places have their pay raised to the level enjoyed by their fellow Canadians elsewhere.
For years governments have been trying to do something about the lower standard of living in Atlantic Canada. If the government would take the simple step of raising the pay of the employees in Atlantic Canada there would be more money in the region.
Simple economics tell us if there is more money in the region, people will probably buy a new car, a new microwave or possibly extend their home which, of course, will stimulate the economy and get dollars moving. That is exactly what we need to have happen.
This week, we will be debating a new constitutional proposal from this government, a document which will outline the principles by which this country operates. One of the guiding principles of Confederation is that all Canadians are equal.
Many of our programs are designed to preserve this equality between people. Medicare ensures that all Canadians have universal access to the health care system, if it is not cut to pieces. Equalization ensures that the have not provinces have enough money to provide the same level of service across the country, again, if equalization payments are not cut to pieces.
Why then is this government treating Canadians differently on the basis of where they live? Two years ago when the ships' crews started negotiating for a new contract, they demanded an end to the regional rates of pay.

that Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee F.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to move second reading of Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan. As part of the government's restraint program, this bill will continue the ceiling on the growth of the federal contributions under the Canada Assistance Plan to the provinces not receiving equalization payments.
Under the Government Expenditures Restraint Act passed last year, a 5 per cent ceiling on transfers to these provinces was set for 1990-91 and 1991-92. The legislation will extend those ceilings through to 1994-95.
Starting off this debate, I would like to remind the House that all Canadians and all levels of government stand to benefit from the wide-ranging measures that this government has introduced to put this country's fiscal House in order.
The federal debt we inherited in 1984, compounded by heavy interest payments over the last six years, represents one of the greatest dangers to this country's social and economic well-being.
Government Orders
Canada's $400 billion debt burden and the deficits that add to it are a national problem affecting all Canadians. It results in higher taxes, inflationary pressure, increased interest rates and, of course, long-term uncertainty. Because interest costs are such a large share of the budget-$43 billion this year or 27 per cent of our total expenditures-the debt consumes funds that might otherwise be used to assist Canadians in need and to support programs Canadians want and reduce taxes.
In sum, Canada's deficit and debt represents a major threat to sustainable economic growth and the ability of this government, and of all governments across the country, to provide the social services that we are so proud of as Canadians.
To effectively deal with this program, we must get back on track in reducing the deficit. This is the threshold step, to get the debt under control and on to a downward path. Deficit reduction requires spending restraint. That is why we brought forward this legislation. It is part of a broad program of spending control needed to establish a positive, economic environment for the country. National problems demand national solutions. For this government to live within its means, spending restraint must be shared with the provinces. Federal transfers to other levels of government are simply too large to ignore in this effort.
Members of the House should bear in mind that for decades the federal government has provided considerable financial support to the provinces and that support, by the way, has grown significantly; by almost 6 per cent annually from 1984-85 to 1990-91. That is a much higher rate of increase than the 3.7 per cent growth in over-all program spending over the same period.
As a result of this growth, total federal contributions to the provinces, both cash and tax transfers, will reach nearly $37 billion this year. The cash component of these transfers will represent about 20 cents of every federal revenue dollar.
We simply cannot afford to let this spending grow without some limits. With this in mind, Bill C-20 has already been introduced to control the growth of Established Program Financing and to provide for other restraint measures outlined in the budget.

Government Orders
Complementing this legislation, the bill before the House today would continue the ceiling on the growth in federal contributions under the Canada Assistance Plan to the three fiscally strongest provinces. Even with the measures that we are proposing, growth in federal transfers is expected to run at 3.7 per cent annually between this fiscal year 1991-92 and 1995-96 in contrast to just 3 per cent for all federal programs over the same period.
The level of CAP spending and the rate of growth over the past few years has meant that we cannot ignore this program as we work to contain expenditures. Since 1984-85, federal CAP contributions have grown at about 7 per cent annually from $4 billion to more than $6 billion last year. In contrast, total federal program spending has grown, as I mentioned earlier, at only 3.7 per cent over the same period of time.
Simply put, this government would not be a responsible custodian of the taxpayers' money if we allowed these contributions to grow without any restraint at all. We cannot spend our way out of problems with money we do not have and funds we cannot borrow except at a veiy high price for us today and, I guess more importantly, for our children tomorrow.
This bill has been carefully designed to balance our concern for needy Canadians and our desire to avoid placing unnecessary burdens on Canadians in the future. We know how important these dollars are in providing assistance to the neediest Canadians. We all know that in our constituencies as we experience it on a daily basis. CAP contributions help provide the most basic requirements of life: food, shelter and clothing, as well as social support in a variety of ways.
To me, the success of CAP is not measured by how many people are dependent on it, but by how many people it can help to regain personal independence. That is the important aspect of this. This independence would be worthless without a healthy economy and the jobs that go with it. It is to ensure the long-term health of the economy, threatened by the debt problem we have inherited, that we must put certain limits on the funds we give the provinces for these purposes.
Bill C-32 is part of a comprehensive responsible plan for fiscal consolidation and economic renewal, a plan based on the philosophy that has inspired this government since we came to power in 1984. We have reformed the tax system to increase its fairness and to improve the international competitiveness of our manufacturing sector. We have reduced waste and inefficiency in government operations. We have taken measured steps to reduce government spending so we can live within our financial means.
We continued our balanced approach to spending restraint even in the face of the recession we have just weathered. We kept to our course because we knew it was the only way to build a stable, long-lasting recovery.
We did not, however, embark on a wild spending spree as many of our critics demanded, especially the former premier of British Columbia, who would love us to just throw money at any problem and try to spend our way out of it. We have resisted the harsh calls from the other extreme, and that is to rip apart the social safety net on which many of our fellow citizens depend.
None of these steps we have taken compromise or will compromise our high, nationally consistent standards for health and social programs. Rather, they ensure that we will have a strong economy, that we will be able to afford these programs in the future and provide opportunities for those in financial difficulty to find independence and self-respect.
The balanced, prudent measures that we have taken, including those announced in the budget last February, will ensure that the deficit this year does not increase over last year, despite the effect of the recession that has just ended.
These measures, combined with economic recovery and lower interest rates, will push the deficit down sharply. For 1992-93, we are forecasting a shortfall of under $25 billion, the lowest in more than 10 years. By 1994-95, we will have eliminated the need for any new government borrowing on financial markets for the first time in 25 years.
During the recession of 1981-82, the government of the day chose a different path, allowing the deficit to balloon by $23 billion from 1982-83 to 1984-85, to a total

September 23, 1991

of $38.5 billion. It is this burden of debt that we have inherited, that all Canadians have inherited from the previous government that has made the legislation we have before us today so necessary.
I would like to assure the members of the House, and of course all Canadians, that the limits on CAP growth do not put this nation's welfare system at risk. The assistance provided under CAP by the federal government will continue to grow in every province. For seven provinces, no gross ceilings on federal contributions will apply. We will continue to match eligible spending on social assistance in these provinces dollar for dollar. In the three richest provinces, CAP contributions will also continue to grow but to a limit of 5 per cent annually. Even with the gross ceilings outlined in this bill, we estimate that during the five-year period in which the cap will be in place, federal CAP contributions to all provinces are expected to grow from $6 billion in 1990-91 to more than $7.3 billion in 1994-95.
CAP contributions to these provinces will continue to grow at a rate that is even faster than the growth in total program spending by this government.
As I am sure all members are aware, we have introduced legislation to restrain the growth in most areas of government spending to 3 per cent annually after the year 1991-92. The three affected provinces are those best able to share in the restraint necessary to build a stable fiscal foundation for this country's economy. Each of these provinces faces interest costs that are considerably less than those of the federal government, and these costs represent a much lower percentage of provincial spending.
For example, the national debt now totals $400 billion-equal to almost 60 per cent of the country's Gross Domestic Product. Interest payments will consume 33 cents of every dollar of federal revenue in this fiscal year
1991-92. In contrast, the combined debt of all the provinces will total about $113 billion this year, or 16 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product, and provincial debt payments will represent about 11 cents of every dollar of provincial revenue. In particular, these charges work out to 11.6 cents of every revenue dollar for Ontario, to 8.3 cents of every dollar for Alberta, and to 4 cents of every dollar for British Columbia.
Government Orders
Before I outline the amounts transferred by the federal government to these provinces, and how these contributions will be affected by the legislation, let me briefly remind hon. members how CAP is administered.
Every month each province and territory sends an advance claim to the federal government. This amount is subsequently adjusted to reflect actual expenditures, and the over-all account is balanced at the end of the year. The annual claim is certified by an auditor designated by the province and accepted by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
While the federal government specifies the conditions under which a particular program is eligible for cost sharing, the provinces are responsible for designing and delivering the programs and ensuring their comprehensiveness. And it is up to the provinces, in this time of fiscal restraint, to ensure that every dollar of assistance is targeted at needy Canadians and not siphoned off by individuals taking advantage of the system. When program dollars are limited, stringent enforcement and monitoring of payments to eliminate abuses is a must.
The actual financial impact of the 5 per cent ceiling on the affected provinces will vary with its level of spending. I see the Liberals disagree with eliminating abuses to the system. The actual financial impact, I repeat, of the 5 per cent ceiling on the affected provinces will vary with its level of spending. We estimate that social assistance spending in Alberta has grown less than 5 per cent since
1990-	91. Consequently, we expect that federal contributions will continue to match the growth in Alberta's spending, dollar for dollar, for that year. The total federal contribution will be about $530 million. For
1991-	92 the federal contribution will reach some $565 million.
For British Columbia, it is estimated that the province will be entitled to about $50 less in federal contributions in 1991 than it would receive if there were no growth ceiling. However, federal contributions will still top $715 million and for 1991-92 they will grow to more than $750 million.
Ontario will receive in 1990-91, $2 billion-about one-third of the total federal CAP contribution. This amount is about $450 million less than it would be if there were no growth ceiling. For 1991-92 Ontario will receive $100 million more for a total of $2.1 billion; by any measure a lot of money.

By taking this measured step we are seeking to live within our means-and the means of the Canadian taxpayers because they are the ones who foot the bill-while still ensuring that those most in need are fully protected. The financial discipline that we are asking for is essential if we are to reduce inflation further and interest rates. It is only in this way that we can strengthen the economic recovery that has already begun.
The fiscal responsible approach we have taken offers the only way that we can generate productive long-term jobs and ensure renewed sustainable prosperity. It is the only way to bring down inflation and create a positive environment in which all Canadians can confidently plan for their future. And it is only by ensuring that we have a prosperous Canada with a sound financial foundation that we can maintain a strong social safety net for Canadians in need.
As announced in the budget, there is a review of all major federal transfers to provinces under way with an eye to improving their effectiveness and tailoring them to the changing needs of the 1990s.
As part of this co-operative agenda the Minister of Finance will be meeting with his provincial counterparts again later this fall. Our goal is to maintain the principles and standards that are the basis of Canadian citizenship, while at the same time respecting provincial flexibility and tailoring services to best meet local conditions.
We are undertaking this consultation not because we lack a strong, positive vision of what needs to be done nor because we lack ideas on how to regain our fiscal balance. Rather, we recognize that for these ideas to be effective they must reflect the shared vision and mutual commitment by all levels of government and by all Canadians.
On the fundamentals of our discussion I am sure there is already full agreement. The success and permanence of Canada's social programs depends on the wealth and prosperity of the country as a whole. I need not remind my fellow colleagues that prosperity cannot be legislated.
As well, I am sure that all members of the House agree that the best assistance for Canadians in need is
meaningful, permanent jobs, and job creation through sound economic management has been a priority of this government from day one.
The government's restraint efforts are even now showing results. The economy began to turn upwards in the second quarter of this year and continues to grow. We are expecting Canada to finish in second place among the G-7 in economic growth in 1992, with a growth rate of around 3.5 per cent.
The positive signs of growth we are now seeing are a source of encouragement, but we are all well aware that many Canadians are still experiencing the effects of this past recession. Without a doubt, we still have work to do to ensure that economic growth continues and that the recovery is sound and long lasting. If we waver, if we let the deficit rise, inflation and interest rates will follow, choking off growth.
We do not intend to let this happen. We have already laid the groundwork for sound economic growth and, if we were to listen to our critics, we would squander the sacrifices Canadians have made so far.
There are no quick, painless fixes to the deficit and debt problems we have inherited; only difficult responsibilities that we owe to Canadians. The extension of gross ceiling on CAP transfers flows directly from those responsibilities. I urge all members of the House to support this motion and to join us in accepting our fiscal responsibility to all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech by my colleague, the minister opposite. What this government and what some of these comments have shown is that the government has not understood that reducing a deficit is not a social or fiscal or economic policy, but a policy that will affect the lives of average Canadians across this country. You cannot replace a fair and satisfactory social policy that prepares looks to the future with a policy that merely reduces a deficit. A government worthy of the name would try to achieve a better balance between economic and social objectives, objectives that are worthwhile, and this means not only acting responsibly, as the hon. member just said-
September 23, 1991



-about not compromising the health of the community, not compromising the economy, finding the way in which one would deal with the deficit.
I listened very carefully to this minister. He talked about the fact that prosperity cannot be legislated. That is true. But prosperity can be foreseen by proper economic policies, fiscal policies and social policies that are married and interrelated one with the other so that we end up with a country prepared to face the future, not frozen in the ideological mould of this particular minister who cannot seem to see beyond the dollars and nuts and bolts of a supposed dollar economy without looking at the people who make up that dollar economy.
I listened with great interest to better understand this government and to find out how this government was going to reconcile its general economic policies with its social policies, with its political policies, with the state of the nation, and in particular with respect to this Bill C-32; this policy of the government with that of keeping this country united, with helping the underprivileged, the underemployed, the unemployed and the poor in particular adjust to the changes that are taking place both interprovincially and internationally in the trade area.
This bill is supposed to deal with the poorest in our country. That is the goal of this particular bill. Whoever wrote the speech for the minister seems to have forgotten what the goal in this bill was all about.
I was curious and hopeful that the current political agenda be not totally dominated by our constitutional arrangement of where, what, and who sits in which rooms of our house. That is important to be sure, but the house is for the people, all people in all stages of their lives as they journey through life.
It is for the people in this house, in our house, which is covered with a common roof, a common set of practical values and that we build the foundation for a solid country where we are going to manage our house for all the people as they move from room, to room, to room, or whether they moved upstairs or downstairs as the world changes around them both inside and outside its borders.
The taxpayers' pocket is one pocket. The federal government in lauding how it has cut its deficit just completely ignores how it dumped that deficit on to the provinces which then subsequently dumps it into the

municipalities. The long-term effect of that is that the same person has three people tearing at its pockets if he or she has any pockets left at all from which to pay the taxes.
Peoples' needs, economic and social, cannot be sidelined with the level of unemployment at 10.6 per cent and higher in certain areas-certainly higher in Montreal-with the level of the underemployed, with youth and immigrants feeling rejected, neglected and depressed, and even with those highly trained and highly educated who cannot get jobs, who move around looking for work. They move to those provinces which seem to be the provinces of higher prosperity: Ontario, Alberta, and British Columbia. They have had the major burden to bear of people looking for jobs as a result of this government's very poor policy.
How government runs and manages its economy has and will have a great impact on how we will want to keep that roof over our heads as a nation. If this is nation building according to this government, I think it is a pretty sad beginning to a very important week in the history of this country.
My theme is one of economic and social policy which go hand in hand; one complements the other. They are not mutually exclusive, and this is what this government does not seem to understand. Given the made-in-Cana-da recession, high unemployment, the free trade agreement that has severely dislocated our manufacturing base, the goods and services tax, and the unemployment insurance changes, provincial social assistance case loads are increasing at a much faster rate, particularly in the three affected provinces where people moved to find jobs that have now disappeared.
I have had some experiences about the impact of this government's fiscal policy. I have seen the street people in Montreal. I have seen those who sleep on the heat outlets, in the doorways. I have seen those who go to a place called Chez Doris-and there are places like Chez Doris everywhere across this land-and other centres where they get a meal. Sometimes they are lucky enough to get a bed. Believe me it touches our hearts; not that minister's but most people in this country. It raises questions in our minds. These people are the visible testimony and the example of the holes that we now have in our social safety net due to the poor policies we have seen from this government.
