With respect to Bill C-32, the act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan, we must consider our concerns about the deficit in far greater balance with the longterm social needs that Canada faces.
We are not here cleaning up a corporate balance sheet for an upcoming annual meeting. This is a country that we are building for the long term.
The Canada Assistance Plan was created in 1966 to permit the federal government to enter into cost sharing agreements with provincial governments for the provi-
Govemment Orders
sion of social assistance and social welfare services for Canadians in need.
CAP is one of the major cornerstones of the social security system in Canada. This program is a reflection of our widely shared values that are at the root of our political culture.
CAP is a service of last resort. It is one to alleviate poverty. The bottom line is that this federal government is abrogating another sacred trust of Canada's social programs. It abrogates this trust by amendments in a small, two-page finance bill.
It has violated the spirit of federal-provincial co-operation which has marked the 24-year history of CAP, and it acted unilaterally for the first time in the history of CAP.
This bill is a companion to that nefarious bill, Bill C-69, which was so capably analysed by my colleague, the member for Winnipeg North Centre. I hope he is feeling much better today. We miss him.
The CAP cuts were just a giant leap backward. It is an unwise, short-sighted counterproductive policy. It is not smart economic policy, which I will debate later.
CAP was designed to address the consequences and causes of poverty due to illness, disability, family breakup and unemployment. It was to be quite simply Canada's war on poverty. CAP allowed Canadians to share in the benefits and obligations of common nationhood and to strengthen their identity within Canada.
What does this bill do? It reaffirms the agenda this government has been pursuing for seven years now, which is to attack the fundamental social safety net of this country that has been established over decades, to pursue a financial debt and deficit reduction in a clearly unbalanced way, ignoring the tremendous social debt and deficit we also face in this country.
Yes, fiscal responsibility is one objective, but along with good social policy we can get a balance. Good government requires a balanced pursuit of both economic opportunity and social justice.
This bill, introduced under the Minister of Finance, implements a measure announced in the 1991 budget and will drain the federal government contributions to CAP by billions. The federal government admits this. You heard it in the speech today; it will save billions in federal transfer payments to the affected provinces over five years, through 1995-96. It will contain at most 3 per cent any potential growth that may be required as we have to restructure and face the internationally competi-

Government Orders
tive world. As I said before, it dumps more responsibility on to the strained provincial budgets. You cannot get blood from a stone. The affected provinces, Ontario, Alberta and B.C., for their part, expect the actual lost dollars to be much higher than what this government has stated. We know how often the Minister of Finance has had inaccurate predictions and has had to correct them after the fact.
The provinces affected by this restraint measure are home to about 46 per cent of the poor families in Canada. Fifty-four per cent of all welfare recipients under CAP live in those provinces; 40 per cent of those receiving welfare payments are children. It is they who will suffer.
Who are the people most affected by this bill? Who suffers the most when government fails to take its proper economic and social responsibility, in balance with deficit concerns, not outside of it? It is the children of this land. If Canada wants to have a strong, creative society tomorrow, it must invest in its children today.
The federal government continually says that it wants to target social programs to the people who are most in need. The capping of CAP will do the exact opposite. It will take away help from the people who need it most, our children. Not only is this inhuman, it is not smart economic policy. To create a productive society and a sound economy tomorrow, we must provide today's children with the tools they need to be creative, contributing citizens. That is why Bill C-32 is entirely counterproductive.
That is why we say, along with the deficit concerns, that we have to balance them with the long-run social and economic goals of this country. That means investing in our children, not cutting back the tools with which they need to live and to prosper in this country.
It is not only children. It is young adults, university students and immigrants who have come here for a new life. It is the whole gamut of underemployed, unemployed and those who fall outside the social safety net who need our help.
The result is that the majority of the most vulnerable people living in this country are very hard hit by this measure. This bill brings into question this government's lack of morality in not treating all Canadians, wherever they live, fairly and equitably.
Of course, the impact of this bill must be added to a similar measure passed as part of the 1990 budget, known as Bill C-69, which cut the growth of the same CAP transfers through 1990, 1991 and 1992 for these three provinces. That nefarious bill, put through on closure, also accelerated funding cutbacks for medicare and post-secondary education to all provinces, jeopardizing the ability and quality of those programs across Canada. In that bill, federal money paid to the provinces for these programs are reduced each year from the 1989-90 level of about $9 billion to zero by the year 2004. However, this government wants us to believe it is taking care of and looking to its responsibilities in building a nation in containing and enhancing this country.
Would you mind telling me what the federal government is targeting for cuts with this measure? I will tell you what they are. Under the CAP plan, the federal and provincial governments share equally in the cost of basic necessities, such as food, shelter, clothing, utilities and household supplies needed by those most in need and the most needy in our society. Only a Conservative could question that these vital programs are luxuries or frivolous or are misused, but that is the conclusion from C-32. That is the conclusion from what this minister's message was this morning.
Under CAP, services are provided for children who are in care or are in need of protection due to abuse or neglect, mentally and physically disabled people, one parent families, the aged, the unemployed, families or individuals in crisis, low income workers, battered women, and rape crisis centres. Do these people sound like the kind of people with the luxury of tightening their belts, as the Minister of Finance keeps saying and keeps espousing? CAP services include essential living services for disabled persons, foster homes for abused children, safe housing for abused women, subsidized child care for low income families and dental care.
September 23, 1991

Many Canadians agree with financial responsibility in government, but do these sound like programs where federal dollars are being squandered or wasted? Hardly I would say. It would take a Conservative to think that way. I would suspect that most Canadians would agree with me.
The restraints in Bill C-32 are bad enough in their own right, but they also confirm once again to this whole country that this government's approach of attacking the most vulnerable of society seems to be a mindset with them. It reminds those at the bottom of the income ladder that Tory times are very tough times. It tells those who today must look to government for a hand to get in line behind this government's crusade against the deficit. It says once again that this government will pursue the deficit problem alone and above all others.
As important as it is to address the deficit, it is only half the answer for a strong, competitive, productive Canada for tomorrow.

In the early 1990s, we have good reasons to fear the destruction of our social safety net, due to this Conservative government's approach.
Indeed, since 1984, this government has pursued a legislative and fiscal agenda that breaks systematically and radically with the traditional values and priorities of our country. For example, we can mention the abolition of universality for family allowances and old age pensions, which are now a thing of the past for thousands of beneficiaries who have to pay them back on their income tax.
There is no doubt that many of my constituents in Mount Royal agree with this observer who said recently that the government seems to have shifted responsibility for social programs from the Department of Health and Welfare to the Department of Finance, which does not have a reputation for very advanced social thinking or for being the government's conscience. Only now, after seven years of this Conservative government, do we start to realize the consequences of this decision to entrust our social policies to economists, lawyers and tax specialists in the Department of Finance.
Government Orders
The government has not yet understood that reducing the deficit in itself is not a social policy.

This government's record in a relatively seven short years stands as a clear rejection of Canada's proud record in advancing the cause of social justice and enhancing our social safety net as a symbol of a caring and just society. Just look back. The forties brought the Unemployment Insurance Act, universal family allowances, the National Housing Act, Central Mortgage and Housing, all steps and all measures to decrease the gap between the rich and poor in this country, something this government has managed to increase.
The fifties also extended the social safety net in this country, including income security provisions for the elderly and for the disabled, 50 per cent cost sharing with the provinces for social assistance payments and a share in the cost of provincial hospital insurance programs. But this is all weeping lilies and weeping willies. According to this government, this is not good social and economic policy for a country. We must have deficit reduction at all costs, it says.
The sixties brought the Canada Pension Plan, old age security, guaranteed annual income and the CAP plan, the Canada Assistance Plan. Through the seventies these programs delivered to Canadians the kind of society they wanted and believed in. The early eighties continued this trend with the Canada Health Act, reaffirming universal medical coverage and an end to provincial extra billing.
Who would argue today that those were not good steps for Canada and every Canadian? Certainly not our Prime Minister. He thought they were wonderful, that they were a sacred trust. Yet this government appears to believe its greatest achievement has been in reversing this proud record and often in sneaky, back-handed sorts of ways. It is never through the front door, never as a policy choice during an election.
This government has seen fit, since 1984, to attack Canada's achievements as a country instead of pursuing a balanced agenda between economic opportunity and

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
social justice. It is an attack that continues through this small two-line bill, Bill C-32.
Canadians will remember the regressive steps taken by this government, cuts to medicare and post-secondary education through the EPF restraints, clawbacks of old age pensions and family allowance benefits, removal of the interest income deduction from the income tax form measure which so helped our seniors, cuts to unemployment insurance programs which affected every part of this country, special fees on student loans that make the burden of education even higher, deindexation of the child tax credits, abandonment of child care, not once but three times, and cuts to housing programs. The list goes on and on.

This bill is only another in a long list of initiatives affecting our social programs that this government has put forward in recent years in the name of budget restrictions and deficit reduction. However, this bill is very representative of the government's short-sightedness in choosing to ignore the many real problems facing us, in order to concentrate all its energy on reducing the deficit.
When I see ministers get out of their luxury limousines in the morning, I tell myself that at the same time hundreds of thousands of Canadians have also got up but cannot go to work as before because they no longer have a job. They are unemployed, thanks largely to Brian Mulroney's government.

This government, as the ministers opposite are whisked off to work, just does not consider that there are families in turmoil out there, families that cannot pay their bills. They are losing their homes. They are sending their children off to school hungiy and they are losing dignity and hope.
This government thinks it is doing the right thing. At least, it has a philosophic bent that seems to be frozen. This government appears oblivious to the plight of the beggar on the street. It is oblivious to the family slipping below the poverty line. It has little feeling for the family that cannot adequately feed and clothe itself.
It is demonstrating all of this in this small little bill. Its aim is to limit the benefits to those in this country who
need help the most. I have told you that 40 per cent of the people being hit are children. These are the people whose children need clothes, bread on their tables. These people want desperately to work, and yet deficit reduction is the top priority of this government. It is important that it be a priority, but not the only one. The Prime Minister has said it is. The last Minister of Finance said it was. The new Minister of Finance says it is. This minister-I do not know of what-says it is.
What the government has not learned is that deficit reduction is not a social policy. Yes, you can ensure that good financial management is among your goals, but it is just one. You cannot substitute good, sound, forwardthinking social and economic policies with only a policy of deficit reduction. You cannot simply use deficit reduction as an excuse to do nothing. You cannot ignore the need for adjustment programs and for sound restructuring policies to ensure a productive, competitive work force in the new global economy.
Good government, to me, requires a vision for people, a plan that puts in place a commitment to that plan that really makes it work. Good government always requires a more balanced and broader approach.
This government has failed to learn that you have to consider, along with the country's economic and financial deficits, the tremendous social debt and deficit that we face now and which will become worse in the future if we do not do something about it now.
These social debts and deficits, whether in education, whether sending a child to school hungry, whether if ignored will grow and be exacerbated in the long run by a narrow vision and no foresight by the government opposite, are the real fundamental issues. We cannot abandon social targets and social policy goals in order to accommodate some sort of blind, narrow-minded view that the deficit should be our strait-jacket.
This government has made the mistake of not forging a balanced approach. This government's economic agenda has stolen from Canadian families any real improvement in their fiscal situations and created massive unemployment. It then makes the poorest in our society pay for it and pay the biggest cost. It then tries to give us an argument that it has created jobs, jobs, jobs, and that it is thinking of the future and it has good plans. It is funny nobody can see it but the government. It is like the emperor without the clothes.
September 23, 1991



By itself, the deficit reduction policy favoured by this government cannot solve our problems and meet our many needs right now in research and development, education, manpower development and retraining. Well thought out and well considered policies are what is needed now. We cannot address appropriately the market's structural problems nor ensure the much needed competitiveness of our manpower on the world markets with inadequate programs. This obsession with deficit reduction does absolutely nothing in terms of improving the skills of a single Canadian worker. This fixation does nothing either for all those people who stand in line at soup kitchens, food banks and shelters for the homeless.
What is needed to address the most urgent of our social problems are clearly defined and effective policies that blend with our economic policies and are just an afterthought.
If we want to build a caring and compassionate nation then people must come first and priority must be given to those in need the men, women and children of this country at the same time as we address the deficit. That is what slipped their minds, they forgot to take that into consideration.
This government believes that we can afford the luxury of waiting until the deficit has been eliminated before considering any assistance to the million and a half unemployed in this country. I say to this government that they are wrong, dead wrong, that we cannot afford such luxury. They also think that they can remain unruffled. Does all that misery not bother them? They concentrate exclusively on the deficit while a growing number of Canadian men and women have to queue up at food banks and while in greater number they have been reduced to begging to survive. Fewer and fewer Canadian children can dream of having a decent future. Their poverty is not only physical but also moral, since they have become hopeless.
I am telling the departments and the ministers who are here today: you are making a mistake. You have strayed. You must get back on track and understand that your
Government Orders
first obligation is not to beat the deficit but to take care of the people you are responsible for. These two responsibilities should be better balanced. One is not exclusive of the other.

This government mistakenly believes that blindly paying attention only to the deficit will somehow magically stop children from having to go to school hungry each morning. It will not. Will it find shelter for the homeless? It will not. I simply say that we do not have the luxury of playing which comes first, the deficit or the strengthening of the social fabric of this countxy and the upgrading of the skills of its people to face the international and interprovincial trades that we require in this country. It is a trade-off this government is making every day and it is totally unacceptable.

You did a few things right, Patrick. I did not say you did everything wrong, but very few things. The disabled in terms of housing are not particularly happy. Come and speak to the disabled and those who are in charge of housing in my riding. Find out what they have to say about the degree and the condition of the infrastructure and the apartments and the housing which you have stopped financing.
This is a provincial responsibility.

Oh, dump it on the provinces again. If you did not keep cutting, the provinces would have the money to do it.
I read the Constitution very well. It is too bad you do not know how to read the Constitution. Your first try was very ineffective. I hope the second one will be much better. We are all hoping that.
While this government is focused so blindly-Mr. Speaker, I will take it up again.

September 23, 1991

Do I have it left now or after? Plus tard ou maintenantl
I know I have discomforted the people opposite, some of the ministers, the minister who is in charge of fisheries out on the east coast and the west coast; the minister who was once in charge of transportation, which is now totally dishevelled and upset. A number of these ministers have recommended that we go through belt tightening, and it is slipping from belt tightening to a belt around the neck for millions of Canadians, choking them now and maybe permanently.
This government uses rhetoric of equality to mask an agenda that widens the gap between rich and poor, through arcane tax changes and the slow elimination of publicly funded programs. This is not acceptable.
In the end, what is this bill? It is one more instalment on the Toiy agenda which Canadians have been living with for seven years. It is an agenda which has as its main focus a sort of blind, narrow-minded preoccupation with the financial debt and deficit, ignoring the social debt and deficit. It is one in which market forces alone are supposed to carry the day and in which survival of the fittest replaces the goal of a caring, compassionate Canada and a more just society.
The result has been an era in Canada in which tremendous social and infrastructure needs have been ignored. The message is that we in Canada have always had a balanced agenda. I suggest that in the end Canadians will agree that deficit reduction fails miserably as constructive social policy or a social policy of any kind.
The total debt and the annual deficit are to be treated in a most serious way. They are real problems. There is not much room for fiscal manoeuvring if that is your only concern. However, relative to other industrial countries I would remind you that Canada spends a much lower percentage of its GNP on social programs. I also think that Canadians agree that you cannot substitute deficit reduction for policies that actually help people.
I do not think that Canadians like the image of people lining up at food banks, of people needing clothing, of people being homeless, of people being hungry. That is the other side of the reality facing this country every single day.
My last words with respect to this national government is that it should start to reflect the concerns of the people and respond to their needs. That is why it was elected. This bill fails to reflect the true needs of
Canada. It reaffirms this government's failure at balancing deficit concerns and our economic and financial deficit with social concerns.
Do not forget that losing a job is for many people a sort of death sentence. The dignity of the unemployed who do not have the choice of working and earning their living honourably is removed.
Mahatma Gandhi was once asked what he thought of western civilization. He paused, and then he said: "I think it would be a good idea". This government would do well to consider a more civilized approach, one that takes into account the concerns I have outlined and accepts its social responsibilities.
I would recommend the government take its ideological blinders off, withdraw Bill C-32 and go back to the drawing board so that Canadians might be again able to look to their national government as a true reflection of the values we share as a people.
It has a fiduciary responsibility for the poorest in this country. That is what the Canada Assistance Plan is all about and that is what it should have done; a more equitable place in society where economic, fiscal and social concerns are part of the national agenda.
I finish with three thoughts. What this government has not learned is that deficit reduction is not a social policy, that to survive in the international and national arenas, we must restore a sense of balance between economic and social goals on our national agenda if we want to build a nation. You cannot substitute good, sound, forward looking social policy with a policy of deficit reduction. Good government always requires a much more balanced approach between economic and social goals for our nation.

I would have repeated this in French had I had the time, Mr. Speaker, but I think that I made it clear and that others will have to repeat it time and time again to make this government realize it has made a mistake and it is going the wrong way. I certainly hope that this country will survive, in spite of the way it is managed and the decisions this government has made.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate. I want to thank the previous speaker for presenting her party's point of view on this current situation. Many of her comments I agree with. I think it is important that we hear all sides on this issue, but I know
September 23, 1991

the government will have its way with this legislation, as it does with its overwhelming majority.
A lot of curious things are said during a debate to bolster an argument. I want to go over a couple of things said by my good friend, the member for Brampton. In making his point the minister said that the servicing of the federal debt took 33 cents of every dollar that Canadians contribute to governments. Then he went on to explain to Canadians why three provinces were under the cap, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
I can speak certainly for British Columbia, but I wanted to make just one observation which seems to be a bit paradoxical about Ontario and perhaps some people might think hypocritical. Since I am in politics I understand the difference between hypocrisy and paradox. Perhaps the Chair could explain how it views it.
In suggesting that the federal government is burdened with having to put 33 cents of every dollar on to the federal debt and rationalizing why there was a cap on Ontario, he said: "They only have to pay 7 cents for every dollar of debt". How can that be when the Prime Minister of this country has gone around scorching the Government of Ontario for its deficit extension of $9 billion when this government is going to have a deficit of $35 billion this year and yet admit that it is paying more than four times per year to service the debt than what Ontario is? Hypocrisy or paradox?
I think the member has been attacking the Prime Minister behind the Prime Minister's back, going around saying that Ontario is paying one-quarter of the debt servicing even though it has a deficit this year that is going to serve people, while it is cutting services to people and paying 33 cents per dollar. Hypocrisy or paradox, Mr. Speaker, I leave it to you to judge.
Second, when this government came into office it said that it was going to campaign to cut the deficit, cut the accumulated debt of this country through deficits. When they came in the deficit was a little over $100 billion.

Two hundred billion.
Government Orders

Yes, $200 billion. They have managed to double it, more than double it, in the time they have been in office.
My friend is quibbling with me about what the federal deficit will be this year. I said $35 billion and he says $30 billion. What was the name of that famous cabinet minister who said: "What's a million?" C. D. Howe said: "What's a million?" These guys say: "What's five billion?"
There is a $30 billion deficit. They have doubled the national debt since they have been in office, and they have the gall to come in here and lecture people on how tough it has been for them to double the debt and the deficit.
All interest.

All interest. Now we get to this cry-all interest. If they wanted to avert some of the problems of internal interest, why in the world did they maintain the high interest rates that were bleeding Canadian businesses, Canadian citizens and Canadian taxpayers in accumulating this debt? Then they come in here and say: "Well, it was all interest". It is like the person who goes out and kills his mother, kills his father, and then goes to court and pleads for mercy because he is an orphan. I find that kind of logic frankly absurd, but it is Tory logic. They are on this maniacal drive to cut back services to people on a right wing agenda that Milton Freedman would applaud. It has gone so far that they make Margaret Thatcher look like Florence Nightingale when it comes to services in this country.
I want to tell you that the absurdity, the paradox and the hypocrisy of this government show no limit. But there is a tender heart in this government's body for one sector of the community. Let us hear it, Mr. Speaker, for the downtrodden corporations of this nation that have been so oppressed under a previous Liberal government, which had a bit of a social conscience-not enough, but a bit of a social conscience. But let us examine the record of this government when it comes to fair share in taxes. Oh, squeeze the little guy, squeeze the GST, cut back in provincial transfers, but let's take a look at just one year with corporations under the Conservative government.
These corporations never have to go in front of a social worker, never have to show what their food budget is,

Government Orders
never have to show what their housing allowance is. They just go on a wink and a nudge between the corporations and this government.
Using the government's own statistics, because I find them convenient, I want to point to just one year, 1987. These figures are from Statistics Canada, before the minimum tax, when you were piling up deficits. Then you were adding to the debt, then you were pouring it on to the debt. You called the Liberals all kinds of names, names that I could agree with for I am not a Liberal, but at least have some decency to admit the names you were calling them had no foundation in fact when you come to this part, of how you have messed up the economy of this country as my colleague said through the GST, through the free trade agreement and now capping the provinces.
I know there are a lot of Canadians out there who will never vote Tory again after I read this information from Statistics Canada. As a matter of fact, there are very few Tories left. Has this government ever pondered why they are at 16 per cent in the polls-16 per cent in the polls? The Canadian people are telling them that they are fed up. Here are some of the reasons why.
I am glad the member is here, and I will send him my autographed notes after because he wants this material to back up his speeches.
In 1987 they had 362,828 corporations that reported $87.7 billion in profit. Now of course that was before the minimum tax. The effective tax rate at that time was supposed to be 36 per cent. That is right. Thanks to a leaky system the effective rate of taxation of these profits was 17.7 per cent. A net of $15 billion was payable. They did not pay their fair share then. They are not paying their fair share now. If we are going to pay down the debts of this country piled up by an insensitive stupid Conservative government, at least make it a fair share. The corporations still are not paying their fair share.
Let me go further, Mr. Speaker. The best is yet to come. Despite combined profits of $25 billion, fully
118,000	corporations, or about one in three, paid no corporate income tax whatsoever. When the debt was piling up because of fiscal policies that were frankly so right wing it made Milton Freedman embarrassed, they were still letting the corporations off the hook.
Tell that to the mother on welfare when she cannot feed her two kids and has to line up in the food bank. Tell that to the unemployed in Montreal and the shopkeepers who have had to close up in downtown Montreal. Tell that to the prairie farmers who are trying to eke out a living at the lowest price wheat in history since the 1930s. Tell them you could not hit the corporations while they
were piling up the debt. There were billions and billions and billions of dollars in favouritism to those corporations, while the average Canadians had to carry the can for their stupid fiscal policies.
Who piled up $400 billion in debt? They did. Who is it that is causing us to pay 33 cents on every dollar on debt charges? They are. Who is it that attacks Ontario because they pay 7 cents on every dollar? They are. Who are the hypocrites, Mr. Speaker? I ask you to ponder that question. I only raise it as a paradox.
I find it less than amusing that this government forces that poor unfortunate minister into a position of defending a policy that is another cut at Canadian federation.
If you want to keep this country together, Mr. Speaker, the way is first of all to come clean about how the debt was accumulated.
Who was responsible for these fiscal policies, and how we are going to get out of it? It is not good enough to come in here and suggest that three rich provinces have to carry more of the can while the other seven do not. We all agree with that. When we bound ourselves together as a nation in Confederation we said in good times in some regions; we would share bad times in other regions.
There is not a taxpayer in this country who would not at any given time understand the need to share right across the board. Under the former Liberal administration there was a move to put a cap on health care spending, to put a formula in on the richer provinces. Ten premiers met with the then Prime Minister and in concert they rejected the formula and went back to the standard concept that a Canadian is a Canadian is a Canadian, and in good times we share and in hard times we expect to be shared with. That concept is being destroyed by this bill. Amid all the flimflam about constitutional debate and regional concerns, this government has made a mess of the economy. They have piled up huge deficits, accumulated debts in this country, and now they are going back to the ordinary people, not the corporations, and saying: "You carry the can". Some regions have to carry it more than others.
Nothing could be more divisive. Nothing could be designed to destroy this country more than the very idea of this legislation. It is not just its application, but in the abstract the concept of this legislation is giving the idea that we will permanently have in this country have and have-not provinces.
That is wrong. That is foolish. We should understand that Canadians are the same from coast to coast and, if you are going to put in Draconian legislation on three
September 23, 1991

provinces, you create divisive attitudes about where you live and regional fairness.
I want to go on to that other group in this country that does not pay their fair share, the chartered banks. In this instance I am not going to savage the current government, but I am going to chide the previous Liberal administration for setting the pattern of allowing the banks to get off the hook. In their last years in office from 1981 to 1984, the Liberals in the same circumstances, moving toward deficits for the first time in large numbers, tried to control the deficit without even touching the banks.
In 1981 to 1984 inclusive, Canada's seven largest banks made profits of $5.37 billion and paid taxes at a rate of 1.34 per cent.
Shame on the Liberals. Shame on the Liberals for giving the banks a break. There is a recession today. That is what they are arguing.
They made it.

They made the world-wide recession? Oh, come now. I can blame the Tories for a lot of things, but they are too incompetent to create a world-wide recession. They have just done it here in Canada. They have only done it here in Canada. They would not have the competence to do it internationally.
To suggest to me that the Liberal's response was to the recession, recession or not the banks made the $5 billion profit. Why did the Liberals not tax them? I know why. When the Liberals are in office they are very right wing. When they are in opposition they are very left wing. That has been the pattern of this country. That is the Liberal schizophrenia that I just had to remind the House about casually when I speak about paradoxes. Should they be returned to office and there is a breath in my body, I will remind them word and paragraph and chapter of the statements they made while they were in opposition. Oh, will I remind them.
Government Orders
Nonetheless, the Tories did not create the recession. What was their response to it? They dug us in even deeper. The high dollar a former minister of Crown suggested was a fixed deal with the United States. Mr. Sinclair Stevens said it and the government denied it. I am inclined to believe Mr. Sinclair Stevens. I have not met the gentleman and so that is why I believe him. I have met the other Tories, so I will pick the one I have not met yet. If I have to do it on that scale it is very easy.
The gentleman said there was a fixed dollar and I agree with him. Why else would the Canadian dollar be going up, up, up like that?
There are lots of reasons.

Lots of reasons. Has the government ever heard of pegging the dollar? Has the government ever heard of the fiscal instrument of leading the nation by saying that the dollar will be traded at x amount?
Is that NDP policy?

Is that NDP policy? I will say this: I would never have signed a softwood lumber deal as dumb as this government did. It pegged the dollar on the day and the dollar was on a rise and there was nothing in the deal to accept or adjust for that rise. Only Tories could make that kind of a decision.
You did not answer my question.

I will. I would peg the dollar. I would also limit interest rates. I would never have allowed them domestically to go the way they did. We would have had a two-level interest rate policy in this country.
Total intrusion in the market. What is the bill? It is a total intrusion in the budgets of the 10 provinces that we are trying to keep together as Confederation. If you say that we are intruding on a market, what in the world are you doing interfering in provincial budgets? The provinces of Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia do not need it. You are giving lessons to the provinces that you will not keep yourself.

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
I find it hypocritical or paradoxical. Back to the banks and what the Liberals allowed the banks to get away with. Not again.
Are you going to nationalize them if elected?
They are already nationalized, only it is a private sector nationalization. Those five banks do not enjoy any competition at all. Try and get some regional competition in banks.
Would you nationalize them?

I would allow the provinces to expand like Quebec has done with the caisse populaire. I would allow the provinces to become far more aggressive as Quebec has done in its economy. Give them some competition. The one thing you free enterprisers do not believe in is competition for those monopoly corporations.
Tell us what you did for them.
We tried to get the Liberals to open up the banking system. I understand that your government may be doing that. If that is the case, congratulations to you.
What do you think of Bob Rae these days?

He just proved the case against Bob Rae. You were not in here. It would help you grow hair.
I will just remind the hon. member of the comparison he gave of Ontario paying 7 cents on the dollar. It is up to 33 cents a dollar and they are cluck-clucking about Ontario. That is hypocrisy or paradox.
The record is replete with how this particular government has made a mess of the economy. It has destroyed almost every one of the fiscal attachments that make this Confederation an attractive place to be for all citizens. It has assaulted the poor and small businesses in this country and then has come along with this bill and said: "Now, you will have to pay for all the insults we have given you".
This government is no longer fit to govern. This government does not have a mandate with the Canadian people. It is not popular in any section of this nation.
I think the best and the healthiest thing that could happen in this country is not this kind of stupid legislation but an immediate election. Let the chips fall where they may.
My God, if a government has ever outlived its time, it is this one. Was it Cromwell who said: "For God's sake, go"? If I may invoke Cromwell, you should have gone months ago.

Mr. Speaker, I am always interested in listening to the member from British Columbia because I share his concern about the banks.
The banks, as he knows, are paying very, very little in terms of income taxes and from all indications have a great many Canadians very unhappy with them.
Will he tell us specifically what his party would do with respect to the banks? Would he nationalize one or all of them? While he is at it, would he tell us why it was that during the three years that he was premier of British Columbia there was such a precipitous loss of confidence in that province? I think he will acknowledge that, or I hope he will because I am a friend of his successor, Mr. Harcourt, and have high regard for him.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, let us deal with the myths about British Columbia.
I will put my seat up against any member of this Chamber who claims that we did not have balanced budgets in the province of British Columbia during the NDP administration.
The fact is we did. We also left $600 million in assets that were later dissipated under the British Columbia Resource Investment Corporation into which poor, unfortunate people were inveigled to invest $30,000 of their funds under a right wing government known as Social Credit. Now BRIC shares are down to about 80 cents.
I can give you a litany of the other assets that were left. The British Columbia Petroleum Corporation. A book which one of the retired executives of West Coast
September 23, 1991

Transmission has written points out that it made $700 million just by marketing natural gas back to the people of British Columbia.
Enough said. If you want to stake your seat on our financial record, do it, but let us put the myth to rest.
The banking system: I personally do not believe that we should buy a bank. I do not believe that, and I do not believe that we should bail out banks either, like the Tories did. In a free marketplace, you have a God-given right to lose money. I find it interesting that they only help the rich when they lost money, not the poor.
What are the alternatives? One of the simple alternatives is to have the logic and the common sense to use internal Canadian financing, just as the Liberal administration started using the Canada Pension Plan in a very, very good way. The step further from the Liberal policy of using the CPP would now be to allow those investors in RRSPs to have access to municipal bonds at 5 per cent and give them a tax credit holiday while the money is in the RRSP and the bond money is being used locally.
There is $90 billion in the hands of the private banks, half of which is only self-directed in the RRSP. If you used the other half and made municipal bonds available-I have spoken on this at some length-it would take that money away from the banks which have nothing innovative at all other than to make massive amounts of profit on interest with no social policy attached.
This is not socialism or free enterprise. This is common sense. Use the indigenous pool of capital that exists in this country to start creating jobs so people can pay taxes and we do not have deficits. People unemployed create deficits because they are not being productive. There is one way.
The second way is to examine the possibilities of Ontario treasury boards, to examine the possibilities of the caisse populaire in Quebec and also the treasury boards in Alberta, indigenous financing for local projects on a long-term basis, the kind of imaginative use of Canadian capital which is not at the vagaries of international capital. It is not offshore borrowing. It is using money here in this country the best we can to buffer ourselves during a recession. It is nothing magical. It is just a little bit of common sense.
The last point is fair shares. Make the banks become competitive by paying their fair share in the tax system. What is wrong with that? Nothing is wrong with it. Also the credit union movement must be strengthened in this country. Extol the virtues of how co-operation among
Government Orders
ordinary depositors can be a powerful instrument in fiscal policy.
None of these ideas has been considered by this government. It makes the ordinary people carry the can while its rich friends get off on a free ride.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member seems to have all the answers to the economic problems facing this country.
Can he explain to me, if his economic policies are so sound, why his government was defeated in British Columbia? Is he suggesting that his economic policies were accepted by the people of British Columbia? Did his economic platform in any way contribute to his defeat?

I love to hear that question from my colleague who is a Liberal member. Five prominent citizens in British Columbia were elected as Liberals. Within months they walked across the floor and sat with Social Credit. They changed their policies by changing coats. They are the ones who defeated the New Democratic Party before the government had a chance to extend itself.
And the people were defeated.

Sure they were. There is no longer a Liberal Party in British Columbia. When the chips were down the Liberal Party in British Columbia went right wing. Four of its members crossed the floor. One of those who crossed the floor was Dr. Pat McGeer who wrote one of the most vicious books on Social Credit, condemning it from head to toe, scandals, payolas and everything. As soon as the Liberals got elected, they joined Social Credit.
While they sat in the cabinet, did they destroy the British Columbia Petroleum Corporation which they voted against and made $700 million for the people of British Columbia? They did not destroy it. Did they destroy the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia? No, they did not destroy it. Did they destroy the Small Development Corporation established by the province of British Columbia? No, they voted against it but did not destroy it.
Every single one of the fiscal initiatives of that government was voted against by those same Liberal members and when they came to power, they kept them and smugly laughed about the profits they made out of them.
I am not cynical. I welcome the questioners question. He is ignorant of his own party's duplicity, but I am just enlightening him a little bit. I would hope that once he gets elected as a Liberal he would stay there, instead of being hypocritical as the Liberals in British Columbia were.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was interesting that the hon. member for the opposition should talk about everything except Bill C-32. Mr. Speaker, I think it would be useful to get back to the bill itself and take a very good look at what this bill is supposed to achieve and consider why the government introduced this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-32 concerns the Canada Assistance Plan, and most Canadians-I think more particularly of the people in the riding of Trois-Rivieres-find it difficult to understand exactly what the federal government does for the provinces and how it all works. Perhaps I may take a few minutes to provide some background.
Mr. Speaker, in Canada, Ottawa or the federal government makes two types of payments to the provinces-the first kind is called equalization, which is probably the better known of the two. Equalization payments go to the so-called less wealthy provinces. Seven provinces receive equalization: the four Atlantic provinces, Quebec and Manitoba. Three provinces do not receive equalization payments: Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
September 23, 1991

There is another program called the Canada Assistance Plan, which means transfer payments made by the federal government to all the provinces. For instance, my own province, the province of Quebec, would theoretically receive two cheques a year from the federal government: one for equalization payments and one for transfer payments to the provinces.
The bill before the House today, Mr. Speaker, applies strictly to transfer payments to the provinces. This bill provides that the so-called wealthy provinces-Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia-will see the annual increase in the amount of money they receive from Ottawa capped at 5 per cent. That is the purpose of this bill. Why? Why these provinces in particular?
As I said before, these are the wealthiest provinces, and in fact, Mr. Speaker, at the rate annual transfer payments to the provinces are increasing, they cost a lot of money. For instance, in 1984-85, the federal government gave the provinces $25.6 billion annually, and this was for all the provinces; in 1990-91, we are talking about $36.3 billion.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia, since 1984 spending by all the provinces increased by an average of 6 per cent. Ontario, for instance, has an average annual rate of 10 per cent; British Columbia, 7.6 per cent; and Alberta, 4.3 per cent. Meanwhile, here in Ottawa, this government has cut increases in government expenditures down to an average of 3.7 per cent annually. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, this government has taken draconian measures to ensure its expenditures do not increase. It has done so, Mr. Speaker, because in 1984, we had a national debt of a little over $2 billion, a legacy from the previous government, and since 1984 that debt has increased. The opposition often says it is all our fault. Mr. Speaker, if the opposition or anyone for that matter were to make a fair and accurate calculation of the increase in the national debt since this government came to power and also computed the annual interest payable on the debt we inherited, they would see the amount is the same. This means that if we exclude the interest on the debt, since 1984 we have managed to control spending by dint of good administration.
In 1984, Mr. Speaker, the federal government spent $16 billion more than it was getting in revenue. This
Government Orders
year, the government will spend $12 billion less than it is getting in revenue. Mr. Speaker, this shows that in seven years we managed to get the administration of this country under control.
However, we still have a problem: the national debt is still there and the deficit is still there, and we must take steps to deal with the deficit and the national debt. One of the ways to do so is Bill C-32, which, I repeat, does not reduce the amount of money transferred to the three so-called wealthy provinces every year. What it does is cap increases in the amount of money the federal government sends to these provinces. The less wealthy provinces which, as I said earlier, receive both equalization payments and transfer payments will not be subject to capping. These provinces will receive the full amount to which they are entitled according to the formula and will not be capped at 5 per cent like the other three provinces.
Another thing we must understand Mr. Speaker, is that the government has frozen all increases in government spending at 3 per cent, until 1994-95, with the exception of transfers to the provinces, while transfers to the wealthy provinces will be capped at 5 per cent, not 3 per cent. Mr. Speaker, you will ask me: Why penalize three provinces? As I said earlier, these are fairly wealthy provinces. We must consider our financial situation. As you know, we often talk about the national debt and the deficit, and as far as the opposition and some Canadians are concerned, it is our problem, not theirs. It is no one else's problem. That is false, Mr. Speaker. The national debt belongs to all Canadians. Each and every Canadian has a $15,000 debt, his or her share of our national debt. It costs the federal government in Ottawa 35 cents of every dollar; 35 cents of every dollar received by Ottawa go strictly to pay the interest on our debt.
Mr. Speaker, Ontario's debt costs that province 11.6 cents per dollar; Alberta's, 8.3 cents per dollar; and British Columbia's, luckily for it, 4 cents per dollar.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, that these three provinces together still pay less interest on their total debts than we do in the federal government. Perhaps they were better run in the past, I agree, but the problem is real. We are asking Canadians to tighten their belts. Mr. Speaker, I cannot imagine returning to my riding of Trois-Rivieres and telling people, "Look, 35 cents of every dollar you send is used to pay interest charges. I would like to raise your taxes a little to be able to give more to the provinces that pay between 4 and 11 cents

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
per dollar as interest on their debt. These provinces are one tenth as indebted as the federal government." We have a social choice to make as a government. We can raise taxes again. I think that no one wants that, Mr. Speaker; you don't want it, I don't want it, Canadians don't want it.
But at the same time, some provinces have low debts, and thus little interest to pay and less to spend on finance charges. Mr. Speaker, those are the provinces that, like the majority of Canadians who are able, must help the federal government solve the problem of the debt and the annual deficit.
Mr. Speaker, that is where Bill C-32 comes in. Again I repeat it, because the difference between equalization payments to the "have not" provinces and the Canada Assistance Plan that benefits all provinces must be understood. The purpose of this bill is to restrict the increase in transfers but not to reduce them. We have heard the opposition say that we were taking money from the provinces. That is false. We are reducing the increase that they would have.
Three so-called rich provinces, Mr. Speaker-and looking at their debt rate, I would call them rich-are affected by this bill: Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think that as Canadians and as people who care about Canada's long-term economic and fiscal health, not simply tomorrow morning but the long term, we must pass this bill as soon as possible.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, allow me to move, seconded by the hon. member for Peterborough:
That this question be now put.

speechtext: Questions and comments. The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier.

Mr. Speaker, it is surprising indeed, but this government has made a habit of imposing a time limit on any debate that bothers or disturbs them in any way.
I cannot understand why this government which has a lot of explaining to do to the people of Canada, a lot of problems to deal with, does not want to discuss this matter and wants to impose a time limit on debate by putting the question. This prevents any further amendment from being made and means that the vote will be taken as soon as we are through debating.
I listened carefully to the hon. member, Mr. Speaker. I have noticed that he has not explained the object of Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan. He talked about the economy, about equalization and many other things. Now, I would have a question to ask him to put in context this much emphasized economic question on which he spent the 12 or 13 minutes of his speech.
Since 1973, Mr. Speaker, assuming that the Gross Domestic Product gives a good enough picture of the goods and services produced in Canada, how can this wealth created by the Canadian people be compared to the national debt? In other words, what is the rates debt GDP?
According to the figures I have-I had the time to do a little research during his speech-in 1973 the debt was equal to 2.7 per cent of the GDP. In 1985, one year after the Tories took office, it was 10 per cent. In 1987-88, it had reached 32.5 per cent. And it is estimated that, by 1995, just a few years down the road, it will be 41 per cent, that is to say that 41 per cent of all the goods and services produced in Canada will constitute debt, Mr. Speaker.
So, I ask the hon. member: Is he defending a good thing or does this economic slump simply go to show that this government is totally incompetent at managing this country on a day to day basis? I ask him candidly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier. We always have interesting exchanges together. However, I have to admit I am surprised by the question, especially coming from someone who has been a member of this House for nearly 25 years-
Nineteen years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Nineteen years then, Mr. Speaker. He comes and talk to me about the GDP, the national debt and the deficit? But, Mr. Speaker, until 1984, his government increased its spending by 15 per cent annually. That is right, Mr. Speaker, 15 per cent a year on average between 1968 to 1984. They increased spending, Mr. Speaker. But revenues were not necessarily coming in at the same rate. That is how we ended up, in 1984, with the Liberal government's credit card limit stretched to $200 billion-not $20 billion, but $200 billion.
September 23, 1991

When this government came into office, it inherited an unpaid credit card bill of $200 billion. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, they were spending $16 billion more than they were taking in every year. So, not only did they leave us with a credit card at its maximum, but they kept at it. In just seven years, by 1990-91, we managed to bring government expenditures down to $12 billion below revenues.
Now, we can take these $12 billion and start applying them toward reducing their debt, by paying their debt charges. That is what is called good, sound management, Mr. Speaker. It is not easy. There were cuts over the past seven years, as you know, and there are yet more to come. Sound management is a must if we want to ensure the future of this country. And sound management requires that we stop spending and start paying our debts.

Mr. Speaker, I would have a question for my colleague. At the beginning of his speech, he mentioned equalization as well as wealthy provinces, referring to the rich and poor provinces of this country. I know that, throughout the proceedings of the Belanger-Campeau Commission, some specialists and so-called economists have argued that rich and poor provinces are really not all that different, except for a few clearly identified cases. But Quebec has always been considered one of the rich provinces and, thus, expected, along with the three other provinces mentioned by our colleague, to provide for the not so wealthy. Could my hon. colleague give us again the objective data?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the knowledge and experience of the hon. member for Outremont. Perhaps I may explain this in simple terms. When the federal government gives money to the provinces, there are two ways it usually does this.
The first is affected by Bill C-32, which we are discussing today, and is commonly referred to as transfers to the provinces. Ottawa gives each province the same amount of money per individual. Suppose this is $10. There are 6 million Quebecers in Quebec so Ottawa will send a cheque for 6 million times $10. There are 8 million Ontarians in Ontario, so Ottawa will send a cheque for 8 million times $10. That is what we call transfers to the provinces.
There is another system for the less wealthy provinces which is called equalization payments, and these are intended to help provinces and their residents whose income is below the Canadian average. The Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Manitoba and sometimes Saskatchewan are eligible for equalization payments. These are computed according to a very complex formula-I don't want to get into the details-but it is based on how the revenues of the provinces compare to the Canadian average. So this is another way the provinces can receive money.
The hon. member pointed out that Quebec is considered to be a wealthy province. Quebec does have substantial revenues. Nevertheless, compared with the national average, it is entitled to equalization payments. I imagine that is what the hon. member for Outremont wanted to clear up.

But this is only the beginning. We must seize this opportunity and actively pursue a settlement. Canadians can be proud of the fact that we were the first country to

September 23, 1991
ask the United Nations to become actively involved in a negotiated settlement of the crisis.
We are pleased that on Thursday a special meeting of the United Nations Security Council will be convened to discuss the situation in Yugoslavia. Today, on behalf of the Official Opposition, I call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs to contact our Canadian ambassadors around the world and the diplomatic corps here in Ottawa, asking them to do whatever they can to urge the United Nations to work toward a resolution of the crisis in Yugoslavia.

Mr. Speaker, if Quebec separates it will assume its fair share of Canada's national debt. According to the Belanger-Campeau commission, that is 18.5 per cent. Other Canadians say it is 25 per cent. Obviously this would be settled by negotiation.
But what happens if there is no agreement? Even if we do agree, Quebec cannot legally assume any of Canada's national debt without the consent of our creditors. Likely Quebec would have to make side payments to Canada for its share of debt retirement and interest.
What happens if Canadian interest rates rise before the debt is paid? What happens if Quebec defaults on its payments? Who knows for sure. What we do know is that the credit rating of both Quebec and the new Canada will be lower than it is for our present Canada and that will hit each of us personally in the pocketbook and reduce our standard of living.

Mr. Speaker, once again Canada is following the FTA rules and getting the back of the hand from the United States for doing so.
This time we are being shafted on softwood lumber. The United States complained about a subsidy. Canadian provinces responded in good faith. Now there is no subsidy and no need for an export tax.
How does our partner in the FTA react? Seventy senators demand that Canada be slapped with a 25 per
cent duty. We have lost trade disputes over steel rails, lobsters, parts of construction equipment and west coast salmon. Even our so-called big win in the pork dispute is a testament to U.S. willingness to back Canadians against the wall even when America's complaint is totally ridiculous.
The FTA is more than we bargained for. We lost 7,000 jobs in the lumber industry. We have seen scores of companies flee south. Over a quarter of a million jobs nation-wide have gone. We have seen our communities devastated by job loss and capital flight. Enough is enough. Abrogate the free trade treaty now and let Canada have a sovereign economy the way it should have had all these years.

Mr. Speaker, an independent Quebec would be economically viable but the price to pay would be relatively high, according to Patrick Grady in a study published today by the Fraser Institute. This economist predicts that Quebec would suffer a serious recession and that Canada would face economic difficulties.
If Quebec became sovereign, the consequences for Canada and especially Quebec could be serious, he concludes in this 168-page study. The deficit of an independent Quebec would increase and its interest rates would rise. Businesses and individuals would leave, Mr. Grady predicts. He says that if the province separates, its economic activity could decline by 10 per cent in the short term and 5 per cent long term. The economic situation would thus be three or four times as bad as the recession that Quebecers are now barely getting out of.

Mr. Speaker, today women in communities across Canada are celebrating the first annual National Women's Centre Day. Single mothers, homeless women, abused women and their more fortunate sisters, can all find strength at women's centres. There they will be met with caring faces, supportive voices, and needed information.
September 23, 1991

Women's centres are at the very heart of our communities. Yet last year this government cut funding for women's centres by 100 per cent and only restored it after a national outcry.
It is clear that women's centres must have core funding. Just having year to year funding is not sufficient. Last week in this House there was much discussion about showing how much members of this House respect women in Canada. Actions speak louder than words. I call on this government to institute core funding for women's centres. That is what will count with the women of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, National Women's Centre Day is being celebrated for the first time today to recognize women who are helping other women to help themselves. Many of these women are volunteers.
By providing information, referral and support services, women's centres play a significant role in identifying and addressing the many problems that specifically affect women and in finding solutions to those problems. They also deliver a wide range of education and advocacy programs which support equality for women.
It is time that we acknowledged their important contribution and help in their financial struggle to keep the doors open. Instead, this government has cut funding to advocacy groups by $25 million, forcing the closure of many of these centres which are already barely surviving on short-term grants and endless fund raising. In fact, in several provinces women's centres receive absolutely no ongoing support from the federal government.
The theme of this year's Women's Centre campaign is "Keep the Door Open for Women". I ask the minister responsible for the status of women to stop closing that door and to implement core funding for women's centres in all regions of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the first official day we recognize the work being done in women's centres across Canada by dedicated volunteers.
The theme of this year's campaign is "Keep the Door Open for Women". In Bridgewater, Nova Scotia, for example, the Second Storey Women's Centre has organized a variety of projects. Sometimes it seems to take a great tragedy to focus our collective attention on the violence and institutionalized inequalities that are faced by women every day in our society. We act surprised and ask ourselves how wanton acts of violence can occur in our modem society. And yet, how can these things not happen when satirical magazines incite their readers to rape young women in the name of humour, and there is little public outcry.
We must work together to change old attitudes and to banish harmful stereotypes. To do this, we must ensure that our centres receive adequate funding from both public and private sectors. I encourage all members of this House to work with the women's centres in their areas to ensure that they have the funding necessary so that women can take back the night and feel safe in their homes and their places of work.

Mr. Speaker, Alain Noel writes in La Presse that the eastern part of Montreal is suffering from a serious shortage of occupational training. Job training is a key issue, says Claude Pichette, president of a committee to revive the economy and employment.
