speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the House of Commons recessed for the summer the problem of cross-border shopping has continued at a significant pace. It is a fact that the large price differential in gasoline between Canada and the U.S. is a major motivational factor in the cross-border phenomenon.
Canadians are flocking to the U.S. in greater numbers, lured by lower gas prices and once they are there they are buying other retail goods.
The severity of this problem is captured in a study done by the consulting firm Ernst and Young on the effects of cross-border shopping. It estimated that retail sales losses to our Canadian retailers is in excess of $2 billion nationally. The Retail Council of Canada put retail losses in Ontario alone at $1 billion in 1991.

This phenomenon cannot go unaddressed. Crossborder shopping creates negative economic activity, especially in border communities like Sarnia.
Both the federal and provincial governments must take a serious look at the taxation of gasoline in an effort to help alleviate the problem of cross-border shopping.

Mr. Speaker, it is has been projected that farm families in the grains and oilseeds sectors will have incomes of about $6,500 for this last year. That is about one-third of what we consider to be the poverty income in Canada.
The previous Minister of Agriculture, now Minister of Finance, promised that his government would provide a third line of defence which would make it possible for these farmers to survive. The government has reneged on that promise.
The all-party House of Commons agriculture committee met in August and unanimously passed a resolution pleading with the government to honour that promise. Today the House will vote on that resolution.
I hope that government members will support the grain farmers by voting for that motion and that governments, both federally and provincially, will extend some hope to those thousands of desperate farmers by taking action now on the third line of defence.

Mr. Speaker, on August 22, 30 organizations from the municipalities of Colchester county met to discuss the area's qualifications as a location for the proposed facility for federally sentenced women. These organizations represent the people who would deliver the services that would provide the benefits that would benefit the lives and futures of the women inmates.
There were members of church organizations, correctional services personnel, law enforcement officers, women's' centres, children's organizations, health workers, emergency measures groups, educators, community
service groups, all levels of government and certainly representatives of the native community, truly an impressive group that showed true community interest in providing a home for this institution and the people who are to use it.
Truro and the surrounding area is an ideal community in which to locate such an institution. It enjoys easy access for the majority of inmates and their families. It can provide low cost accommodation for visiting families. It is a positive community with a positive people who will provide assistance and be role models as these women move back into society.
I urge the Solicitor General to approve Truro as the site of the Atlantic women's correctional facility because it is simply the best place for it.

Mr. Speaker, these are confusing times to be a Canadian and to be debating the possible breakup of our country.
On the one hand there are people telling us that if Quebec leaves Canada, we would probably all be better off. Certainly that is the message of the Bloc Quebecois and the Reform Party.
On the other hand, groups such as the Fraser Institute are now warning that Quebec separation would mean a stock market crash, higher interest rates and a deep recession for all parts of Canada, including my riding.
I do not know who is giving Canadians the best vision of the future. Canada should not stay together just out of fear. I ask all Canadians to stop and think about these two conflicting positions. Whichever they end up choosing, they will at least have taken some action to form Canada's future instead of just letting it happen. Hopefully, Mr. Speaker, they will choose Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the 1991 fishing industry along the northeast coast of Newfoundland and Labrador will be recorded as disastrous, potentially the worst in memory.

September 23, 1991
Oral Questions
This failure is mainly the result of heavy pack ice and icebergs which persisted in some areas until now, resulting in cold water temperatures that disrupted the inshore fishery and the migratory presence of cod, capelin and other species, and the continued plundering of transboundary stocks by foreign fleets. The impact on those communities dependent on the fishery is devastating.
Inshore landings are considerably less than one-half what they were last year and, as a result, thousands and thousands of fishermen and plant workers are without their incomes. Their incomes have been wiped out and there is not enough work to qualify for unemployment insurance.
These are extraordinary conditions and they require extraordinary measures. I join my colleagues in the Liberal Party in calling on the Conservative government for a comprehensive strategy on aid to those engaged in the fishing industry in Newfoundland and Labrador who are in dire need, and for an immediate response to this crisis.

Mr. Speaker, this morning, Consumer and Corporate Affairs launched the second annual Kids Care Week. I know this Elouse shares my dismay that approximately 400 Canadian children die and some 54,000 are hospitalized each year as a result of accidental injuries. Kids Care is a response to this tragic reality.
During Kids Care Week, events will take place all across Canada to reach out to communities and to parents to raise awareness of every day dangers and to stress the message of Kids Care. Children are our most precious natural resource. We must do what it takes to keep them safe. I applaud this vitally important program and wish for a very successful Kids Care Week.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow the government will table its constitutional proposals. I would like to warn the government that constitutional change will be difficult to implement in Canada if the government does not show Canadians it also understands the need for rapid economic change. In the present context, Canadians are not feeling very generous. I therefore ask the Minister of Finance and Deputy Prime Minister, considering the fact that the unemployment rate is rising instead of going down, what kind of concrete measures the government intends to take to reduce the number of unemployed Canadians which today reached 1.5 million.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the key to bringing about growth in the Canadian economy is the reduction of interest rates, and the key to reducing interest rates is bringing down inflation and inflationary pressures. Both have happened and to the extent that has had a positive impact upon the economy, we have seen growth emerge in the second quarter on an annualized basis of 4.9 per cent. We expect that growth to continue, albeit in a modest and moderate way because there are some other difficulties that exist within the Canadian economy, namely, the balance sheets of corporations and a burden of debt overhang, as well as a shortage of credit available to consumers. So it is tempered with that.
The important issue is to get the fundamentals right. We are getting the fundamentals right. Sustained growth and price stability can occur through the containment of inflation and fiscal consolidation. That is the policy we are following, and that is the policy that will produce results.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these are the policies the government is following and these policies are not working. I want to tell the government that 1.5 million unemployed Canadians will not be swept under the rug because we are again beginning the constitutional debate.
September 23, 1991

I want to serve notice to the government that we will not let it off the hook with its very bad economic policies and with the mess it has created in Canada.
My question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Now that we have the free trade deal, when will we see the adjustment programs that the Prime Minister promised to Canadians during the last election in order to face the problems they have today as a result of losing their jobs? The government's promise to give them help is not being fulfilled.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are existing programs within Employment and Immigration which have been very effective in terms of providing adjustment measures. The government has provided adjustment in the fisheries sector, the agriculture sector and the shipbuilding sector. All of these things have occurred.
I do not know whether the Leader of the Opposition has decided to support or continue to oppose the free trade agreement, but I want to tell him that in Edmonton the other day Dow Chemical announced that it was going to build an $800 million petrochemical plant. The president and chief executive officer, Mr. Wilcock, stood on the platform and said: "Ladies and gentlemen, this facility would not be built here had it not been for the free trade agreement because it has reduced tariffs and given us access to the marketplace." Now, is that what the hon. member is opposed to?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance that there are farmers in Canada who are waiting for help from this government. There are fishermen who help from this government. There might be the creation of a few jobs here and there, but there are hundreds of thousands of people who are losing their jobs because of the mismanagement of this government.
I would like to know if the government will soon present us with an economic plan because we not only need a constitutional plan, but an economic plan to keep this country together.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member, who was the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board, and has had some interest in this issue, will find it very revealing, when he sees the document, that we are taking some very important steps in terms of strengthening the economic union.
I think that will be very positive. I think it will allow for a greater degree of fiscal and monetary co-ordination which I think is necessary in this country. If we are doing it at an international level, surely it has to be done at a domestic level as well. I think that we can build on that.
I agree with the hon. member that the unemployment rate is too high, but I also ask him to remember the fact that over the last six years this country has had the best job creation rate of any nation in the OECD. It has had the second best growth rate. It is the seventh largest economy and the seventh largest trader in the world, and we intend to maintain that leadership.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, who likes to cite facts. Well the facts are that in eight of ten provinces, unemployment went up not down in August.
The minister knows as well that in six of ten provinces, unemployment exceeded 10 per cent in August. He also knows that unemployment hit a six year high in August, and yet he declared the recession over. Unbelievable.
I want to ask the minister whether 10.6 per cent unemployment, 1.5 million lost souls in Canada, is now the acceptable level of unemployment in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one likes to see a level of unemployment that high. I do not, and the hon. member does not. It is not as simple as just simply snapping your fingers and all things come into place.
The German electronic giant, Siemens, wants to quadruple its 3,000 strong work force within the decade.

Where?

September 23, 1991
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Oh, where. "A large number of these jobs would be in Ontario," Mr. William Waite, President of Siemens Electric of Mississauga, said yesterday. He said: "There is one catch, the jobs will materialize only if Ontario can generate enough skilled people able to use the latest technologies. My problem is not with an 88 cent dollar, my problem is with the lack of skilled workers." That is clearly part and parcel of the problem. While we have one million plus people unemployed, there are many jobs that are available but they are not filled because of the lack of training and skills that needs to be provided. That is an issue that is being addressed by the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and it is one that is going to require the co-operation and the partnership of all components of society.
Mr. Speaker, I am from Newfoundland, not Disneyland, and I recognize a Mickey Mouse performance by a Minister of Finance when I see it.
Hear, hear.

Does this Minister of Finance not realize that it is very difficult for 1.5 million unemployed Canadians, for farmers in need and fishermen in need, to be tolerant and generous toward this government and its policies, including regrettably its constitutional policy, when the Minister of Finance has shown nothing but contempt for the unemployed of Canada?
I ask the Minister of Finance: Will he produce an economic plan to help put this country back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government has created an economic climate that has produced the best job creation rate of any country in the OECD. We have gone through a recession. The recession has been deeper than was originally expected. We are coming out of it. We are going to have, we believe, sustained growth in the order of 2.5 per cent, achieving 3.1 to 3.5 per cent in
1992.
According to the OECD and other informed observers, it is pretty clear that this country is on the right track in terms of its economic and fiscal policies. We intend to follow that because it is the only way that we can build an
economy that will provide sustainable growth with price stability. That is our goal. That is our objective.

My question, Mr. Speaker, is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The Deputy Prime Minister has just said that they have the best job creation program ever. One and a half million Canadians are asking: "Where is this job from this job creation program?"
The Deputy Prime Minister says we are on the road to recovery, but the statistics say something else. Last week, the international trade figure, particularly our trade with the United States, was the lowest in 10 years. Today, we see that retail sales are still at the recessionary level. The Deputy Prime Minister knows that what this means is lost jobs for Canadians.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister redirect his economic policies so that we can get Canadians back to work and stop just catering to the powerful and wealthy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member knows that there is a certain lag time. When there is growth that is recorded in the economy, there is a lag time until that is translated into jobs. That is what we are seeing.
With respect to her point with regard to the merchandise trade balance, I remind her that in the second quarter exports grew by some 22 per cent. It is not that exports have fallen, but that imports have increased because of the influx of machineiy and equipment to gear up for the demand that is being created. I think that is what has to be taken into consideration.
Obviously, the recession, as I said, was deeper than was expected. It is going to take a little longer to get out of it. We cannot remove ourselves from addressing the fundamental issue. The fundamental issue is that we must contain inflation. That is the trick to bringing down interest rates. Interest rates have come down by 5.5 percentage points. That trend is continuing. The spreads have come down and that trend, hopefully, will continue. That is the way in which we will get the economy back on its feet again.
We are convinced that there will be sustained recov-eiy, but there must be price stability at the same time.
September 23, 1991

Mr. Speaker, the only trend that is continuing is that unemployment remains in double digits and more than 1.5 million Canadians remain out of work. That is the trend that is continuing, despite what the minister says.

I have another question for the Deputy Minister, who keeps reciting the same old statistics. What does he have to say to employees at Angus, Kemtek and Dominion Textile in Montreal? What does he have to say to employees who have lost their jobs like so many others in this country? What does his government have to say to all these unemployed Canadians? What does it have to offer: statistics or jobs?

Mr. Speaker, I can inform the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party that the Conservative Party has done a great deal for Montreal. And since she wants some facts, I can inform her that today, Merck-Frosst is investing $239 million in current research activities in the pharmaceutical sector. According to the company, this major project was a direct result of the passsage in 1987 by the government of Bill C-22, which enhances protection of intellectual property rights in the pharmaceutical sector. This measure encourages businesses to invest in major research and development activities in this country.
We supported Bill C-22. Where was the New Democratic Party when it could have done something to help Montreal?

I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker. This is good publicity for the government, but it doesn't produce jobs for Montreal's unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. The Prime Minister has said that a Constitution without a vibrant economy is "just a pretty piece of paper".
As we enter another round of constitutional discussions, many Canadians across this country including the ones we have just been speaking about, those without jobs, are preoccupied just with survival, with putting food on the table.
Oral Questions
What real economic option such as jobs or a child care program is this government prepared to bring forward so that those Canadians who are living in need can have their basic needs met, can have a job and a decent child care program? Then, they can work together on the unity of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sympathize with the points that are made by the hon. member.
I take no comfort in having an unemployment rate of more than 10 per cent. I also recognize that the hon. member disagrees with the fiscal and monetary policies that the government is following. That is fair ball, but I think that she should recognize the fact that the OECD, which is an international organization, did its report card on Canada and said that it endorsed Canada's monetary policy as being necessary.
It was very supportive of the fiscal policy action and the thrust of the February budget. It was very supportive of the structural policy changes that we have brought forth, i.e. the free trade agreement, the Foreign Investment Review Agency and the GST.
All those things were necessary, including reform with respect to the unemployment insurance program. They were critical about our ability to be productive and in terms of our labour efficiency. They were critical about our unemployment insurance program that they considered was too generous, so we take this as an objective assessment. The hon. member should not ignore that.
Mr. Speaker, my question is this: The vast majority of Canadian economists believe the Canadian dollar is overvalued by at least 6 cents. Does the Minister of Finance agree?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada does not have a set exchange rate for the dollar.
It is established in the marketplace. The hon. member can have an opinion on that, but it is established in the marketplace. There are many factors that are taken into consideration, i.e. capital flows, interest rates, inflation rates, merchandise trade balance and all those things. The hon. member should know that.

Oral Questions

Everybody knows that the value of the dollar is as a result of a series of conflicting factors, but it is also clear that this government has tilted the balance the wrong way.
As a result, it is fighting inflation on the backs of the unemployed and it is pillaging our export industries. I did not ask the minister why the dollar is up there; I asked him whether it should be up there.
The vast majority of Canadian economists thinks it is over-valued by at least 6 cents. Do you agree with him?
I appreciate the brevity of the question, but I would ask all hon. members to put the question through the Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member can have an opinion about the value of the dollar.
The value of the dollar is established in the marketplace. Quite frankly, if the hon. member believes that the dollar is over-valued by 6 cents he might want to enlighten me as to how he would bring the dollar down by 6 cents. How would he keep it there?
I think Canadians will realize-
Resign.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
The hon. member says "resign". I am not a finance minister who is going to come along with simplistic nonsensical solutions that will not stand up to international scrutiny.
* sic *

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. During the last two weeks, 2,300 Canadians lost their jobs at Air Canada, Canadian and Nationair, in addition to the 3,000 jobs lost last summer.
Today's reports indicate that the government at the open skies negotiations is on the verge of giving full cabotage rights to American carriers, full accessibility in Canada.
Given our industry's serious state of health, the continued loss of thousands of jobs, there is the fact that our industry is so much smaller than the American
industry. I ask the minister how the government can even contemplate offering American carriers full accessibility across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's concern about the airline industry in Canada, just as we have concerns about it.
The reason we entered into the negotiations with the United States was to ensure a more viable service between the U.S. and Canada where Canadian industries could get a larger share of the pie.
The hon. member mentions that we are going to put that on the table and I am sure he is getting that from an article in The Financial Post, but I would also like to quote what was said by the speaker referred to in that article: "Canada presented a paper on cabotage at the third exploratory round which outlined controversial aspects including legal, technical, and regulatory implications and, in particular, conveyed the economic concerns raised by Canadian stakeholders that cabotage should not threaten the viability of Canadian carriers".

Mr. Speaker, that is the same talk that Canadians heard before the federal government entered into the free trade agreement, and now those same Canadians are paying the price.
I go back to the same minister: Given that an all-party committee, including Tories, and most of the industry is flatly against cabotage, will the minister categorically state in the House for Canadians that during the open skies negotiations, the Canadian government will not sign an air agreement that will give Americans full cabotage rights in Canada? Yes, or no?
Mr. Speaker, this government in its agreements with the United States will not sign anything that is not good for Canadian airlines.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Transport.
I want to remind the minister that the current imbalance between Canada and the United States shows a favourable balance of $500 million a year on the Canadian side. This is not something we have to get into in order to protect our carriers.
September 23, 1991

I also want to remind the minister, through you Mr. Speaker, that we have seen thousands of Canadian workers in the aviation industry thrown out of work in the last year alone, that the airlines are operating in the red, passenger loads are down, and the only solution that this government has come up with is to turn over our domestic and international travel to the Americans.
I want to ask the minister what is in these negotiations for Canadian airlines and Air Canada, if anything.

Mr. Speaker, the very reason we are in negotiations is to make sure there is a better share for Canadian airlines. In the transporter market, we have not given away cabotage. We have not signed an agreement. We are in exploratory talks.

Mr. Speaker, the article this morning in The Financial Post made it very clear that not only was cabotage now on the table with the agreement of the Canadian negotiators, but that Canada offered up the so-called fifth freedom, the rights of the Americans to stop off in Canada and pick up Canadians and take them on to a third country.
Given the fact that we saw during the free trade negotiations that this government cannot be expected to work on behalf of the Canadian people, and we are now seeing what is happening with the open skies negotiations, I want to ask this minister, through you Mr. Speaker, if it is not now time to do what the Americans did a number of years ago and walk away from the table while we still have a domestic industry.

Mr. Speaker, the fifth freedom rights are a standard agenda item for any international discussion, whether it be with the United States, with the United Kingdom or with any other country.
We will walk away from the table when the agreement is not good for Canada. We will stay at the table until we get one that is good for Canada.
Oral Questions THE ECONOMY

Mr. Speaker, this morning Statistics Canada reported that retail sales for July were down from June, were down substantially over May, and were down 5.3 per cent over the year.
Just last Friday in this House the Minister of Finance declared, and I quote: "Consumer confidence is up". Can the minister explain how consumer confidence can be up when consumer purchases are down, or was he just wrong?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the statistics that I have show that consumer confidence was up by 11.7 per cent and business confidence was up by 17.3 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, that is so-called confidence that is not expressed through the dollar and through purchases. Canadians are not prepared to put their money where the minister tells them they should be putting it, because they have no confidence in him.
In spite of lower consumer spending, in spite of a ten-year record fall in the trade surplus, and in spite of rising unemployment, our dollar continues to go up. How many more jobs must be sacrificed in the name of this government's economic policies? Just how much unemployment is too much for this government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure what the official policy position of the Liberal Party is. The hon. member who just spoke said that the dollar was over-valued by six cents. I am not sure what the other hon. member who has just asked the question considers the dollar should be. I ask him this: If he has an evaluation, he may want to explain to the House how he would establish that figure, how he would be able to reach that particular figure, and how he would be able to keep it.
Is the hon. member proposing a fixed exchange rate? If he is and if that is Liberal Party policy, why does he not come clean and tell us what he is talking about?

September 23, 1991
Oral Questions UNEMPLOYMENT

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
The Deputy Prime Minister knows full well that this government's policies, including the high interest rate and the high dollar, have been responsible for the loss of at least 209,000 jobs in Ontario alone since March 1990. When will the Deputy Prime Minister realize that you cannot have reconciliation in this country if you ignore the unemployed in Canada?
When will he implement the adjustment and retraining programs which were promised over and over again, both during the last election and immediately following it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while it is true that there have been some substantial job losses during the course of the recession, and I think in the manufacturing sector that has been the predominant case, but when it is compared to the recession of 1981-82 I think the decline in manufacturing at that period was about 19 per cent and the decline in manufacturing during this period was 11 per cent.
The peak to trough decline during this recession was about 2.8 per cent; the peak to trough decline in the 1981-82 recession was 5.5 percentage points.
Mr. Speaker, we are coming out of the recession. Growth has been registered in the second quarter. That is one-quarter sooner than we had projected. Growth will continue in the third and fourth quarters, and all reliable accounts would lead us to believe that there will be growth in the range of 3 per cent to 3.5 per cent in
1992.	Now, that is cause for optimism and that is cause for confidence.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a week ago the Deputy Prime Minister stated that the recession was over. Now he is saying we are coming out of it. Have you changed your mind?
Right on. He does not know if he is coming or going.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Let me remind the Deputy Prime Minister that-
I want to remind hon. members to put the question to the minister through the Speaker. The hon. member can finish her question.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask if the Deputy Prime Minister has changed his mind. Just last week there was an announcement of another thousand jobs that were being lost in Toronto at McDonnell-Douglas. When will the government stop ignoring the unemployment disaster that it has created and implement new training and retraining programs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what I said and what I will say today is that we have experienced a growth of 4.9 per cent in the second quarter on an annualized basis. We expect growth to be in the order of 2.5 per cent in the third and fourth quarters of this year. We expect growth to range in the area of 3 per cent to 3.5 per cent over the course of 1992. Those are figures that are supported by the OECD and by many other economists. That will give us the fastest growing economy in all of the G-7, if not the OECD.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I have just returned from the CSCE conference in Moscow where we heard first hand about the very serious economic crisis which faces the people in the Soviet Union this winter with widespread shortages of food, power and medical supplies. As Alexander Yakovlev has said: "Empty pans are more dangerous than tanks".
I want to ask the Minister of Finance: Will Canada now show leadership in the G-7 by supporting the urgent request of Soviet leaders, including the Prime Minister, mayors of Leningrad, Moscow and others for major food and other aid now to avert this looming crisis facing the Soviet people who showed such courage, as winter approaches?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leadership for the co-ordination of this particular initiative is in the hands of the Prime Minister of Great Britain, John Major, who is the current chairman of the G-7 group of countries. He has been there. My colleague, the Minister for International Trade has been there, our deputies have been there. They are looking at ways and means of
September 23, 1991

putting together a package, but also, more important, looking at ways and means of distributing such food aid, medicines and other support measures. What is really important is to establish the mechanism.
I think, as the hon. member knows, that the system for distribution is not very sophisticated. Unless there are mechanisms to ensure that the aid, food and medicine get to the right people at the right time, it will go of little value. That co-ordination is taking place and Canada is very much a part of that exercise.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the same minister. Five years ago the tragic explosion at the nuclear reactor at Chernobyl resulted in thousands of deaths and widespread illness, environmental damage and homelessness in Ukraine, Byelorussia and Russia.
Given this devastation, will Canada respond positively to the urgent appeal which was made last week at the United Nations General Assembly by these republics for a $646 million fund to help eliminate radioactivity from the food chain and to resettle the homeless victims of the Chernobyl disaster?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can report to the House that in my meeting today with members of the delegation of Ukraine, the president, the minister of health and others, we discussed the exact issue that the hon. member has raised. I pointed out to them our interest to help.
The hon. member would know that on September 20 there was a pledging conference in which Canada participated. I would also draw to his attention that through the World Health Organization and the International Atomic Energy Agency, we have been using our participation and membership there to help.
I also have instructed my officials at the Atomic Energy Control Board and will speak to AECL on whether or not we could help in a technical way the people of Ukraine. The last point I would like to make to him is I discussed this at the IAE at my recent meeting in Vienna, as well as with Canada's membership of the working group of the European Energy Charter in which we are now responsible for chairing the nuclear working
Oral Questions
committee. We look forward to very close co-operation with the delegation and the people of Ukraine.

Mr. Speaker, when the Quebec caucus met in Riviere-du-Loup in August, members from the island of Montreal presented a study on Montreal's economic situation. As chairman of the Montreal caucus, I have a question for the minister responsible for the Montreal area.
Could the minister tell the House about the government's latest initiatives to give back to Montreal its assets, its economic advantages, and to restore it to the place it always held and should still hold?

Mr. Speaker, let me reply on behalf of the minister responsible for the Montreal area who is now with the Prime Minister in Montreal, where Merck-Frosst will announce this afternoon that they will invest over $200 million, raising the number of researchers from 200 to 300. Mr. Speaker, that is a direct result of a policy of this government.
Were it not for this policy and Bill C-22, we would not have had that investment in Montreal. It is thanks to that policy. Mr. Speaker, we know that the situation in Montreal is difficult; we know that very well, but we will try to improve it with policies like Bill C-22.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question for the Deputy Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister has asked for the co-operation of the national parties in this House when it comes to the Constitution. The government has asked for our good faith and it has pledged to us the spirit of non-partisanship.
In that spirit, the Leader of the Opposition has agreed to be briefed on the government's constitutional proposals this afternoon at 4.30 p.m.

September 23, 1991
Oral Questions
Will the Deputy Prime Minister please inform the House, at what time they brief members of the Business Council National Issues?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (President of the Privy Council and Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs; President of the Privy Council

Mr. Speaker, before I start my speech, I first want to wish one of our colleagues, Mr. David Walker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, a speedy recovery.

I understand, David, that you are under the weather but let us hope that our main critic on this subject matter will be here before this debate ends.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House is not an extremely complex piece of legislation. It consists of a single section whose purpose is to amend the Canada Assistance Plan. The bill proposes to extend the 5 per cent capping of increases for transfer payments under the Canada Assistance Plan from two years to five. As you know, Mr. Speaker, capping applies only to those provinces who do not receive equalization payments. I am referring to Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Canada Assistance Plan is to help the provinces provide welfare payments and services to the needy as well as social welfare services aimed at relieving, eliminating and preventing the causes or effects of poverty, child neglect or welfare dependency.
Mr. Speaker, this is a worthwhile program that is part of our Canadian way of doing things, part of our national fabric, a program that is extremely important because it enables those who are better off to help those in need.

The Canada Assistance Plan is our safety net of last resort. It makes it possible for provinces to provide basic
income to close to two million low-income Canadians. These people are in this situation, not by choice but sometimes because they just cannot get out of it. They were bom into it and they are having an awful time trying to get away from it.
Many low-income Canadians have been forced out of work, cannot find a job and have used up their unemployment insurance. They must apply for social assistance under this program.
According to government estimates, the three affected provinces, Ontario, Alberta, and British Columbia, will lose $2,135 billion in federal transfers over the next five years, that is from 1991 to 1996. Provincial estimates are much higher than that. Ontario, my province, estimates that the cap on this Canada Assistance Plan will cost Ontario $1 billion this year alone.
The premier of Ontario in an interview reported in The Toronto Star on August 16, 1991, is quoted as saying: "Ontario cannot afford literally to put up with the notion that in times of recession, which has hit Ontario harder than anywhere else, that our citizens are going to be even more vulnerable than others".
By moving with Bill C-32 the Conservative government is leaning toward the new social services proposed by some right-wing groups, the Reform Party among others, which call for a reduced government role in social services and leaves the burden to non-governmental agencies, business volunteers, families, assuming all the time that the government's share of carrying this load is not a public responsibility.
We in this party disagree strongly with the policy put forth by our right-wing partisans in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her question.
I wish I were in my office. I have a paper there which I read recently which said that the rich are getting richer and the poor are getting poorer.
To sustain that statement, it showed that the rich have more disposable income today in 1991 than they had four or five years ago. That is possibly due to some Tory policy. Maybe that is the name of the game, but the poor's share of the national pie, if I may call it that, is going down.
I am saying to this government: Show some heart. Be caring about Canadians. Do not cut into the social programs of this country. It is the wrong thing to do.
Over there I know there are sensible people who have their hearts in the right place. I appeal to them to vote against this bill because this is the start, the erosion, of our national framework of understanding among Canadians and that basically is that we share the good times and the bad times. We should share with those who are having a hard time at this time. There are 1.5 million unemployed out there, and possibly .5 million who have left unemployment insurance because they cannot get it any more.
My colleague from Gander-Grand Falls knows all about that because he has a high unemployment rate in his riding. It is a sad state of affairs when you cannot get a job. That is what Canadians are asking for, not more, not less. Get them a job.
Here we are talking today about cutting into those programs which help those people who cannot get a job, who have no unemployment insurance but have to depend on social assistance programs. I hope this government comes to its senses and votes negatively on this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter the debate this afternoon on Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan, which in effect will extend to 1995 the 5 per cent cap that has already been imposed upon federal transfer payments in the social welfare and social services field.

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
The government brought forth the original bill and is now bringing forward Bill C-32 with the argument that this will help the country somehow turn around this horrendous public debt which it has accumulated over the years, will reduce the current account deficit and, through fiscal restraint, will put the government books back in order.
On the surface this is a compelling argument. Whenever you mention the evils of debt to individuals, to families, to family heads, you immediately get a very positive response and people will agree that debt is a bad thing, that debt has a very negative impact, as we say today, on one's emotional or psychological health, and that debt is something that drags the family or the individual down and drags a nation down.
Nations have been living with debt for a long time. While I am not saying that debt is a good thing, I think we have to look at the causes of debt and a whole variety of ways of dealing with its reduction. I will get to that in a few minutes.
As I approach the main subject of my address this afternoon, I wish to remind my hon. friends of certain characteristics we have developed in this country with successive governments down to but not including the present one through which we have established a way of life in this country, at least until a few years ago, that was considerably different in many respects from the way of life of our American friends and neighbours to the south.
We have chosen to put community first. We have chosen to use government fiscal policy to redistribute wealth. We have chosen to establish programs financed by the federal government to assist people to cope with day-to-day problems, problems related to public education, problems arising out of the concerns of those who manage public transportation, public health and health care, which we call medicare in this country, and the social services in the country to help those who are less fortunate or who fall upon adverse times in their personal lives, such things as workers' compensation at the provincial level, unemployment insurance at the federal level, even to the point of using federal funds to retrain people for the ever changing work place.
All of these things cost money. In Canada, at least until a few years ago, Canadians were prepared to pay the bill through their taxes, whether they were federal or provincial or municipal taxes. In the last two or three years this whole assault on the public debt by this
government, revolving around fiscal restraint to bring down the public debt, has created a fear in the country that we cannot spend anything any more, or that these very worth-while programs have to be curtailed or reduced and some actually eliminated.
I do not think the people opposite, our colleagues on the government benches, really understand the social impact, to say nothing of the emotional or psychological impact, that this deficit fighting is having on our country. While we may be reducing current account deficits a little bit each year, the public debt in this country on the one hand is increasing. It is now estimated that it will be at least $400 billion by the end of this fiscal year and possibly $420 billion. On the other hand, a lot of these social programs that made Canadians different from the United States are now being subject to market force constrictions or marketplace limitations.
In other words, this government wants to treat social problems the same way as a corporate financier or a corporate manager would treat a corporate problem.
I am suggesting to you, Mr. Speaker, that that cannot be done because what is happening-and I have said this before in other speeches similar to this one dealing with social and economic issues-is that this is leading to an assault on the middle class. It is leading to an assault on middle class institutions. Public transit, for example, is being destroyed by government policies. VIA Rail is one specific example, as is the cabotage problem in terms of the airlines and the privatization of Air Canada. These are basically middle class institutions.
In our public school system, while we do not see decay at this point, we do see a tremendous negative impact in terms of financing. What the federal government does not provide directly or indirectly from Ottawa the local ratepayers are having to cough up at the municipal or local levels in order to keep their schools open and their high schools functioning.
We have the problem of public education. We have medicare, where it is being suggested that user fees be introduced in order to defray a portion of the cost. I can afford user fees, but medicare was originally used to help all of the people, particularly the disadvantaged and low income earners as well as the middle income earners. When you bring in user fees all in the name of fiscal restraint, you are mounting yet again another assault on
September 23, 1991

a community based program. The community here of course being the entire country.
This government is doing everything it can to attack the middle class and middle class institutions. You may think this is somewhat outrageous, but all one has to do is look at what is happening in the United States with the same marketplace orientation to solving social problems. There you do see the decline of public transit, of public schools, of public or state universities and colleges in some areas of the United States.
Of course they have never been able to come to grips with public or state sponsored medicare. That is why you have such a divergence in private insurance programs in that country.
By way of introduction I simply want to say that we should be very careful in assessing the psychological, emotional and social impact of legislation such as Bill C-32, all in the interests of sharpening our pencils and balancing budgets. A country is not made up entirely of a budget. It is not made up entirely of dollars and cents. It is made up of people who have people problems, and we have to bring more to those problems than simply an accountant's approach, more than just a business approach. There are some things in this life that the marketplace cannot handle. The marketplace cannot handle many of the social programs that we and our predecessors on both sides of this House have fought for for years to improve the standard of living for our fellow citizens.
I cannot help but see in Bill C-32 yet another plank in this government's right wing corporate agenda. It is just one more piece of evidence that the corporations, the tax system, the rich in this country are not going to be hurt or hindered by this deficit-either the national account, the national public debt or indeed the annual current account deficit. It is really an attack on those least able to cope with the financial problems, both at the personal level and at the national level today.
The 5 per cent cap on government spending on social programs through the Canada Assistance Plan continues, but we have been running inflation rates in excess of
Government Orders
5 per cent for the last two or three years. Some have come in just about 5 and then 5.2 per cent. The deficit this year is expected to go as high as 6 per cent on the total annual basis.
How does this impact on the provinces? If the inflation rate is 6 per cent and the cap is at 5 per cent and we are in a recession where more people are unemployed, there are lower tax revenues coming in at the provincial level and lower corporate tax revenues coming at the provincial level. It means that the provincial governments, particularly Ontario which has been hardest hit by this recession, as well as Alberta and B.C., will probably have to borrow. In fact Ontario has had to borrow on the public money markets in order to find the funds to pay the increase in costs for these social measures.
And we saw a deficit budget that came in, in Ontario last May, projected to go as high as $9.7 billion. But of that just one item, $1.6 billion, was the direct result of the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan-$1.6 billion. There was about $2 billion that the previous Liberal government had not even accounted for. There is about one-third of that budgetary deficit right there.
I suppose Canadians would not mind all that much if everybody were asked to pay his or her fair share of taxes in order to cope with these deficits. But that is not the case, as you and I know, Mr. Speaker. For example, during the years 1986, 1987, 1988 and 1989-four boom years in this country when corporate profits increased by 34 per cent-the corporate taxes in this country declined by 20 per cent. Now we are not expecting corporations to pay higher taxes during periods of economic downturn, when sales are down, productivity is down, when they are going through layoffs, adjustment or rationalization programs or whatever the buzzword is now. But those were boom years, four or five years in this country when profits soared by 34 per cent and corporate taxes went down, down, by 20 per cent.
But during those same four years those in the second lowest income bracket, the second lowest quintile I think they call it, saw their personal taxes go up by 1.1 per cent. In the highest quintile, the highest 20 per cent of income earners in this country, their income taxes went up by

Government Orders
only .9 per cent from 1986 through 1989 inclusive. The second highest group went up by only .3 per cent.
Now, is that tax reform? Is that the way it should be? Should those who are in the lower income bracket see their taxes go up the highest while those in the upper income bracket see their taxes go up at a much lower rate? That is not tax reform. That does not give credibility to this government. That is one of the major causes for discontent in this country today and one of the major reasons why this government is stuck at 12 or 15 or 16 per cent in the polls.
It is because of the unfairness of the government's programs. It masquerades as reformers, and when you cut through all the fancy words and language you find out that whatever the reform is it is not fair. What it is doing, either in the name of fiscal restraint on the one hand, or in promotion of the private corporate sector, the private corporate sector is not paying its fair share of the costs.
For example, Bill C-32 is going to slash transfer payments to the provinces in the field of social programs, but of this whopping deficit that we have only 6 per cent is caused by spending in the social envelope. According to Statistics Canada-and that first figure I gave was from Statistics Canada-tax breaks to the rich individuals in this country and to the corporations accounted for 44 per cent of the debt in this nation. Today, those rich people in this country and those corporations have the same loopholes of tax deferment that were existent in the laws of the land 10 or 15 years ago. They can still shelter their taxable incomes and they can defer spending their taxes forever and ever. Corporate lawyers know this.
There is no point talking about a minimum tax in this country. We have not got it for that matter, as long as you have tax loopholes where you can defer paying your taxes. Corporations still list tax deferments, not on the liability side of their annual reports but on the asset side. They are using tax deferments as an asset. Nothing can be more blatantly obvious as proof of my argument.
This government is misleading the people of this country again by saying that we have to tighten our belts in the social envelope to get the debt down, and yet only 6 per cent of that debt is caused by spending in the social
envelope of social programs and 44 per cent of the debt is caused by tax breaks to the rich and by corporations being able to defer and write off all kinds of moneys that normally should go in the form of tax revenue to the federal government.
What we are seeing is not only an assault on middle class institutions and middle income earners and low income earners, but this is having a very negative effect on the people as a whole. They are turned off by government. They are turned off by lies by politicians. They are turned off by duplicity. They are turned off by programs that are supposed to be reform programs but turn out only to be masquerading as reform programs, bringing in more and more unfair and inequitable pieces of legislation that affect people differently. The rich are getting richer, as the saying has always been, and the poor are getting poorer.
This Conservative government seems to be powerless to do anything about it. It knows its time is running out, perhaps at the most a year or a year and a half to go in this Parliament, and it refuses to see and appreciate the problem. We also realize that this particular Conservative government under this particular Prime Minister is probably the most ideological Conservative government, in fact the most ideological government I would suggest that this country has had in the 20th century, certainly since R. B. Bennett. I do not think there is any question about that. If it does not fit the marketplace then it does not fit period; that is its motto.
Privatization, deregulation, the free trade agreement as it was written, the GST which is a tax that hits everybody equally at 7 per cent-it could be 9 per cent or perhaps on the eve of the next election it might even be 5 per cent-are all measures that will actually widen the disparity between those who possess and those who do not possess, between those who have a reasonably comfortable life and those who have a life of constant struggle.
Is it any wonder that the premier of Ontario, not in an ideological way but in the interests of promoting national unity, has suggested that transfer payments, medicare and social programs are just too damned important to be left in the hands of any one single government, that they should be enshrined in the new Constitution, and that we should have a social contract or a social clause in our Constitution?
September 23, 1991

It is not just rhetoric. It is not just words. It would at the very least give all Canadians, rich and poor but particularly the poor and the middle income earners, a guaranteed vested interest in that Constitution to make certain that the Constitution comes forward and that we maintain national unity in this country, whether it is francophone or anglophone, whether it is in New Brunswick or in Alberta.
That is what this party is pleading for. That is what the premier of Ontario is suggesting. I commend it to this government and to the Prime Minister and to the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs.
I see that my time has run out, Mr. Speaker. I thank you very kindly.

Mr. Speaker, I think my question will become more or less a comment because the member in his speech has probably answered all the questions that anyone has in this House.
I know the members across the way have not been looking up, have feigned their disinterest and are working away at what they are doing. I know perhaps that they are somewhat embarrassed and ashamed because they certainly would concur with what my colleague has said about the clawback on old age pensions and the end of universality as we know it.
I pay particular attention to the medicare that we are so very proud of in this country. It is so ironic that just the other night I was watching a program that came from the United States narrated by Walter Cronkite who suggested that one in four bankruptcies in the United States is a direct result of medical care: one week in a hospital, $10,000. One in two Americans do not proceed to get the attention that they would require for their medical problems for fear that they cannot afford it. Twenty-five million Americans cannot afford any insurance. Lo and behold, if you do get ill and access the insurance program, you can surely bet that they will cut you off in short order.
It seems strange that we are cutting our medicare program or taking a very serious look at that through user fees, and the Americans on the other side are trying to emulate us. They have actually studied the program and said we are more efficient: "We would like to have what Canada offers". This is sold under the guise by the party in power that it is not an attack on social programs. It is just that we are going to spend more wisely.
Government Orders
The member pointed out the competitive agenda, the market driven agenda. This government says that it is the have provinces that we will not get the transfer payments for. We will reduce transfer payments to Alberta, B.C. and Ontario. I do not know if Ontario can be considered a have province. When you do not transfer to the province then the province must transfer to its municipalities. In the case of my municipality or the riding that I represent, Sault Ste. Marie, just last week the province of Ontario had to give $4 million to the city of Sault Ste. Marie just for back taxes that the Algoma Steel Corporation cannot pay.
The feds just say: "Oh, well, it is provincial jurisdiction because Ontario is well off". We resent that statement very much.
As far as the social contract is concerned, the European Economic Community suggests that a social contract is in order. Why would we not have one in North America?
Before I lose the good graces of the Chair, I do not know if the member would want to elaborate any more on what he has already done.

Mr. Speaker, very briefly, I think the main reason why the European community has been able to insert the social contract into the constitution of the European community is because of one man, Mr. Jacques Delors, who I believe is the president. Mr. Delors also happens to be a French socialist. He was determined that the European community would not be dominated in its economics and its economic dynamics by countries like Germany or his own country of France or the United Kingdom or Italy, or the more advanced if you like. He was taking into consideration families and workers, men and women in countries like Portugal, Spain originally, and Greece.
He said: "We do not want to create an economic union here and a trading pact where great multinational and trans-national corporations can trade off countries, where they can say fine, we will locate in Portugal if we can get labour burden down to $5 an hour U.S. We will relocate from Germany down there for the cheap wages". "No", he said, "we are going to contract up so that the poorer countries in Europe will be able to pay higher wages and will stimulate their economies and

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
their standards of living upward so that nobody can take advantage of and exploit the poorer countries in that organization".
We are in negotiations now with Mexico. I have nothing against Mexico. I love it. It is a beautiful country and I love Mexican people. It has a dynamic culture. What are we doing? We are not putting any safeguards in there for our working families or for American working families. Trans-national corporations are doing it now, racing down to Mexico to exploit Mexican workers at a much lower cost or labour burden to them, which is going to have a profound disruptive impact on the Canadian and American labour markets.
In Europe, Jacques Delors said: "We do not want that and they are not going to get that". Here we are in North America, falling prey once again to that corporate agenda of which our Prime Minister is a slaving supplicant. He sees nothing else but that in his thinking.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise to participate in this debate today on Bill C-32, an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan.
I have listened with great care and interest to the remarks of my colleagues on various sides of the House. I cannot help but think that there is a fair bit of misunderstanding as to what is going on, not only in this House but in the government, with the finances of the nation. I could not help but be impressed as I prepared these remarks in reviewing the progress that the government has made over the last seven years in coming to grips with an extraordinary financial mess that it inherited seven years ago from its predecessors.
I have to say this as a member from rural Atlantic Canada, an area that benefits tremendously from federal government expenditures, an area that is greatly concerned about the unity of our country because the breakup of our country would leave Atlantic Canada isolated from the rest of the country. We are highly dependent on the Government of Canada.
That is one of the reasons that we are not too thrilled at the kind of rhetoric that is coming out of the Reform Party these days, when it talks about reducing expenditures across the board by 10 per cent and when it talks about getting rid of things like ACOA, reducing equalization, reducing veterans pensions and old age allowances. My goodness, we are talking in this debate here about capping the Canada Assistance Plan, the growth and expenditures to three provinces so that they can only grow by 5 per cent. We wonder what would happen if the Reform Party and Mr. Manning came into power and everything was cut by 20 per cent. It is a pretty scary prospect for Atlantic Canadians, I must say.
What we have here is a piece in a very well ordered and well structured financial plan to bring back into order the finances of this nation, to ensure the confidence that is so essential in controlling things like interest rates, the rate of inflation and the value of the Canadian dollar that ensures the flow of investment to this country, investment that is the basis for jobs.
There are not walls around the country, but investment and sound finances. Those are the things that are important.
This bill is part of a financial package that really began in 1984, but most recently follows in line with the budgets of 1990 and 1991. I must say I commend it to all members of the House as we come to consider it here today, and indeed in the days ahead.
I think it is important to remember that the finances of this country were very much out of whack. In 1984, we had achieved an accumulated national debt of $200 billion.
Even more frightening was the fact that the national deficit was $38 billion. It had been allowed to run rampantly out of control. That $38 billion actually included a $16 billion operating deficit.
It is important to understand the structure of this debt. The government of that day was actually spending $16 billion more each year than it was taking in. In addition to that, it was paying $22 billion in interest on that $200 billion national debt.
I have people say to me: "What progress have you people made on the deficit? You have only brought it down from $38 billion to $30 billion." On the surface that is true, but let us look at the structure of the debt.
September 23, 1991

We are now running the government on a $12.5 billion surplus. That is a $28.5 billion turnaround. How has that turnaround been achieved? A certain amount of it has been achieved through increased revenues resulting from tax reform.
Some would say, by increasing taxes. I am not sure. It is more a question of taxes reflecting the growth in the economy. Even more important, it has been achieved through a 70 per cent reduction in expenditures by the Government of Canada.
That is management. That is tightening the belt. That is leading by example. I heard some of my hon. friends earlier saying, as some people say: "Ah yes, but the national debt has doubled since you people have been in power. What accomplishment is that?" Of course, they are hoping that nobody will dig a little more deeply to understand the structure of that debt, because it is a very simple thing.
If you take a debt in 1984 of $200 billion and you do nothing towards bringing that debt down and if you take, say, an average interest rate of 10 per cent per year even though the interest rates were much higher in the early 1980s, even in 1989 and 1990. Through the sound management of this government, I am pleased to note that interest rates have gone down 5.5 per cent in the last year, which is going to be of great benefit to the Canadian economy.
If you compound a $200 billion debt for seven years at 10 per cent and if you just add it up, what does it get you? It gets you $389 billion. If you want to be a little more accurate, it is probably about 11 per cent, then you compound it and you end up with a debt of $415 billion.
Members opposite say that this government has doubled the debt. This government has not doubled the debt. This government inherited a $16 billion operating deficit, turned it around to a $12.5 billion operating surplus. By getting the finances of the nation under control, we are gradually going to get at that $400 billion debt that is the legacy of the Trudeau Liberal government to Canadians.
Thank goodness we have had a government which had the courage and the integrity to tackle that debt. There is no question. Every politician in this House knows that it is much easier to get yourself popular by giving money out than by taking it away. That is the situation.
Government Orders
When we talk about capping the Canada Assistance Plan, what exactly are we dealing with? Speaking from the perspective of an Atlantic Canadian where we are so highly dependent on things like equalization and transfers to the provinces, it is very simple.
If the Government of Canada is going to tighten its own belt, if the Government of Canada is going to do something-

Mr. Speaker, there is really no need to apologize. It is quite a legitimate point of order.
My good friend from South Shore is in full flight and all that, but I am sure he would want to recognize that in the energy of the moment, he misled the House.
He talked about a $400 billion legacy of the Trudeau era. He will be aware that the public debt at the time his cronies took over was $180 billion. It is now $400 billion.
