speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure my hon. friend from Burin-St. George's will wish to perhaps make his point, invalid though I happen to feel it may well be, when we come to the questions and comments. There is no question that if you take a $200 billion debt-actually it was about $199 point something billion in 1984-85, so my hon. friend might check the budgetary figures and then come back in time for questions and comments and he can make his point.
I would invite him to compound the interest for the last seven years on that debt that the government of which he was a member, left as a burden to the taxpayers and the young people of this country, and come back with an accurate figure of what that debt is, if he wishes to try to dispute the reality of the fact. What we are left with as Canadians is roughly a $400 billion debt. That is a legacy of the government of which he was a member. However, he can come back with the accurate facts and figures if he believes that mine are not accurate.

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
I was saying before this euphemistic point of order was raised that in controlling expenditures, if roughly 25 per cent-maybe it is 24 per cent or 26 per cent; I would not want to run afoul of my hon. friend opposite- of the expenditures of the government are in fact transfers to the provinces, then what is more reasonable than if we are going to confine expenditure growth, that it should apply equally to transfers to the provinces as to the expenditures and the programs of the Government of Canada itself.
It is important to note that it is not as if this government has not significantly increased the transfers to the provinces. For example, this year total federal transfers to the provinces in cash and tax points will be some $37 billion, up from what was $25.6 billion in 1984-85, which is an average annual growth rate of 5.5 per cent.
At the same time, federal government program expenditures have gone up an average of only 3.7 per cent. This government has asked nothing of the provinces that it has not done in greater measure to itself.
Costs cannot be controlled unless expenditures are controlled. Indeed, if the provinces are not prepared to control their expenditures, but simply feel they can rely endlessly on the Government of Canada to meet their shortfalls, maybe it is appropriate in the interests of the taxpayer that the Government of Canada exercise some control and then leave the provinces free to go beyond that if they so wish.
I listened with interest to the premier of Prince Edward Island on the radio the other day. By the way, he is in contravention of a federal-provincial agreement, refusing to provide legal assistance to anyone charged before the courts. Indeed, there was some suggestion that it would be appropriate that the premier of Prince Edward Island, who is also the attorney-general, be cited for contempt of court. He made the statement in what seemed to me a semi-serious attitude, you know, an unhealthy semi-serious attitude, that what difference does it make if the federal government has a big debt? So what if the federal government has a big debt and the provinces do not have very big debts. So what. The federal government should just continue to let their debt grow. It is all the same taxpayer, he said, it is all the same taxpayer.
Well, if it is all the same taxpayer, let the province that wishes to spend the money, generate the money and
answer to the taxpayer for it. This government wants the taxpayer and wants people beyond this country, the investors who are so important to the future of this country, to know that this government acts in a fiscally responsible manner and is going to endeavour to control the expenditures that it brings down.
Are the social programs of Canada put under siege by this government? Some, of course like the immediate speaker before me, the hon. member for Brant, suggested that social programs are under attack. I would suggest that we are not going to have social programs in the future if we bankrupt the nation. At what point does the nation cease to have the ability to govern itself when your national debt is a third of your expenditures as is the situation now? Is it when it is 50 per cent of the expenditures? At what point does the International Monetary Fund come in and say you are not responsible to govern yourselves?
Those are questions we might ask.
The accumulated debt of the provinces in this country is considerably less than the accumulated deficit which was estimated at $30.5 billion last year. At the same time that of the provinces is $9.4 billion.
Where is the Canadian taxpayer federally? You know 33 cents on the dollar is going to pay interest on the debt. What are the situations in the provinces? The average is about 11 cents on the dollar. It would seem to me that we need to tax the provinces which are not paying their fair share. When we look at the provinces that are impacted by this legislation they are not the provinces that are in the greatest financial need. It does not include provinces like the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan. What is the situation in those provinces? In Alberta it is 8.3 cents, 11 cents in Ontario, and 4 cents in British Columbia. That is the percentage of expenditures that goes toward the debt. Yet they say that the Government of Canada should continue to run up a debt.
Maybe that is why the Government of Canada has run up a debt because of uncontrolled spending by the provinces.
It is interesting to note that the figure 9.4, which is the combined deficit of the 10 provinces of Canada, is soon going to be blown out of the water by the actions of our friends in Ontario, Mr. Rae and his spending approach. It is going to be interesting to watch. As a Nova Scotian, I am greatly concerned about what happens in Ontario

because Ontario has such a major impact on the economy of this country as a whole and indeed on the economic numbers. Things like inflation and interest rates are driven very largely by what goes on in Ontario.
The message is going out across the land that the Government of Ontario is going to spend, spend, spend with no regard for where the money is going to come from. The Government of Ontario is determined to put that province and the future generations of that province in a financial situation such as this country might have been in had there been no change in approach. If the $38 billion deficit that was inherited here in 1984-1985 had been allowed to continue, we would have a deficit of some $100 billion in this country today. I suspect that if Mr. Rae does not come back down to earth and recognize that he has to exercise some responsibility in the way he governs his province, what we are going to see is Ontario doing its best to rival the federal government in the size of its deficit.
I do not know what the future of that would augur. It will be interesting to look at the reaction of businesses to the proposals in Mr. Rae's budget. I cannot help but wonder what we can expect down the road. I heard earlier today one of my hon. friends from the New Democratic Party pulling out the old saw about the free trade agreement leading to lost jobs. I wonder if he is going to be prepared to stand up and honestly face this House as businesses leave Ontario running from Bob Rae and his approach to economics and the potential impact that they are going to have on the economy of that province.
As new industries, such as the one the Minister of Finance was speaking about today, and new opportunities develop in this country, and as our economy generally becomes stronger I am sure that my friends opposite in the New Democratic Party will continue to try to find opportunities to blame anything that goes wrong on the free trade agreement, even though there is no validity to it whatsoever.
Coming back to the bill more specifically, I think we should take cognizance of the fact that what we are talking about here is limiting the growth of expenditures. We are not talking about cuts. We are talking about limiting the growth of expenditures. There will be no limit on the growth of expenditures in the provinces where the need is greatest. But there will be a 5 per cent ceiling on growth in the three most affluent provinces, at
Government Orders
a time when it is important to note that the Government of Canada as part of its budget is also limiting growth in expenditures in federal government programs to 3 per cent. What we have going down here is that the government is being far more generous to British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario than it is being to itself.
What constitutes unreasonableness? Some provinces have resources at their disposal, limited deficits that they either have or inherited when they came into power and limited tax dollars that they have to allocate to paying interest on their debts. If they feel that their growth should exceed 60 per cent more than the federal government is allowing them and the federal government is allowing themselves, then let them find the resources for the revenues.
It amazes me how often I listen to people in this place and elsewhere suggest that the government should spend more money here and spend more money there. They say: "Let's expand this program. Why are we limiting expenditures here and limiting expenditures there? Are they proposing that we further increase the federal deficit, or are they going to propose new tax increases or new taxes?" Sometimes my friends from the NDP will say: "Tax the corporations". That is the solution to every problem. Bob Rae is going to find out he won't have any corporations left to tax if he keeps going the way he started out. There has to be an element of realism. That is what this government has provided, in the way of financial policy, an element of realism in its approach.
The Tories in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
It is very interesting. I should not allow myself to be distracted, but I do wish to comment. One of the really excellent things that has happened in the last year is that we have a government in Nova Scotia under the leadership of the hon. Donald Cameron. It is tough to stand up and take the tough measures, to do what seven governments have responsibly done, one of them being Nova Scotia, and indeed what the Government of Canada has done. We feel that we have a responsibility to the person who pays the piper and that is the taxpayer of Canada, whether

they be from Newfoundland, British Columbia or anywhere else in between.
It would be nice to be able to say spend away all you want, there is no limit to the bottom of the well, but unfortunately there is. We have a government in Canada, a government I am proud to support, that is standing up for Canadians, future Canadians as well as present Canadians, in seeing that our finances are brought under control. One of those areas is the Canada Assistance Plan, and I encourage all members of this House to join me in supporting this excellent bill.

Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the hon. member's speech. However, I want to remind him of just a couple of things.
He accused Premier Rae of spending, spending, spending. The reason why the deficit in the province of Ontario increased so quickly in one year is twofold: (1) the previous government had hidden the facts of the decline in revenues to the tune of about $2 billion and (2) this government, by pulling back through the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan, cost them another $1.6 billion.
But the point I want to make is this: I would like to ask the member how he accepts the fact that this plan will tighten belts and help to reduce government expenditures so that they can get the deficit under control, as he put it, when he knows that under present tax laws $6 billion a year go untaxed at the corporate level in this country-$6 billion.
Second, would he tell this House who would he ask in the province of Ontario to pay for the 14 per cent increase in welfare? Ontario has been severely hit by recession, has lost somewhere in the neighbourhood of
300,000	jobs, largely because of free trade and the high dollar that has been imposed on this country by this government. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course I listened. My hon. friend asked many questions. It is difficult to know where to begin, but I am glad to see that he has not forgotten the rhetoric that has been sort of the gospel of the New Democratic Party for the past three years.
The member says 300,000 jobs were lost from the free trade agreement. I would like to see some accurate estimates of those figures. It is very interesting. I noticed those figures came from a study done by the Canadian Labour Congress. I am really intrigued with the fact that if you look at those figures and you break them all down, you see jobs lost in the Atlantic fishery included there. Is that not interesting? The number of fish in the ocean decreases and guess who is to blame? The free trade agreement.
Some of those job losses are in the tobacco industry. Significant thousands of Canadians have ceased to smoke, so the demand is less. Blame that one on the free trade agreement.
The big area, of course, that the NDP likes to talk about are the reductions in the automobile industry which, of course, are not a part of the free trade agreement. They have the auto pact to look after them.
We can talk about the brewing industry which is a part of those numbers. The brewing industry is explicitly left out of the free trade agreement.
My hon. friend, it is like anything else, you hear enough figures and you know enough of them are wrong that you wonder about the other ones.
My hon. friend is looking for a comment on the dollar and I would be pleased to comment on the dollar. There are two ways to deal with the dollar. I have to tell you, in all honesty, my particular constituency is highly dependent on exports to the United States. I honestly have to tell you that we, on the south shore of Nova Scotia, would very, very much like to see a substantially lower dollar than we have today, but what do we do? Do we have the Government of Canada decide the value of the
September 23, 1991

dollar or do we do it the way it is supposed to be done? The dollar is high because people outside this country have so much confidence in this country. Is that not a remarkable turnaround from what I hear from my friends opposite.
When we talk about exports, the lower the dollar of course the more we can sell. However, we have to look at competitiveness. We live in a new world. We do not live in the 19th century. We are moving rapidly toward the 21st century and we have to be ready to compete. We have to look at our own productivity. We have to look at wage rates. We have to look at how many people are involved in the process.
They talk about pricing differentials between Canada and the United States and they like to blame it all on taxes or something like that. Well, taxes might be a little piece of it. You then look at the amount of profit taken by retailers, the amount of middlemen along the way, the cost of production, but it is great to be able to poll something in isolation and say: "Ah ha, that is the problem, there is the bogeyman."
The reality with the dollar is that the dollar is high because of international confidence in the Canadian economy. You do not have to take it from me. Look at the reports of the OECD and other internationally respected bodies that look at these things. The fact of the matter is that the high dollar hurts us right now in some areas where we export, particularly exports based on our resources, but it also challenges us as Canadians to become more competitive.

Mr. Speaker, I do not suggest there is any hope that the member is going to answer any of the questions from this side of the House.
If we can get back on topic with regard to the free trade agreement and social policy, it was the Prime Minister who said that the free trade agreement would enhance social programs in this country. This is a redundant debate and a redundant bill. It is totally unnecessary.
Getting back to the question from the member for Brant, he said: "Who is going to pay in Ontario?" I cite my community again where the federal government said: "Here is a CAP." Sault Ste. Marie, in dire straits, the largest employer in the community cannot pay municipal

taxes, $4 million. Who is to pay? The province transferred the funds to the community. The federal government does not participate.
Sault Ste. Marie is not alone. In northern Ontario the unemployment rate is 15 per cent. Who pays? I want the member to answer that question. If the federal government is not going to participate, what role is it going to play and who pays?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
I will very briefly answer, Mr. Speaker, because I know our time is just about up. There is a very simple answer to the member's question. The taxpayer pays.
The question is, at the same time the Government of Ontario must manage its affairs with the resources that are available to it. If the demand on the Ontario government in this particular area is greater, well then maybe it has to take a look at expenditures in other areas. That is exactly what this government has done. That is what the individuals you speak of in their homes have to do. That is what I have to do in my home. If I spent 15 per cent more than I took in every year, I would be in real serious trouble.
You have got to cut the cloth according to the pattern. The answer is very simple. The taxpayer is going to pay. It is just as well that it be the taxpayer or the guy making the expenditures as somebody else's taxpayer, but the bottom line is that the public is saying to the governments of the day and to this country: "Live within your means just as we have to as citizens".
I suggest that the Government of Ontario needs to learn that lesson. It could have no better model than this government and the Minister of Finance who is with us here right now.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words on this legislation which is called an act to amend the Canada Assistance Plan. In effect, what it does is reduce the amount of money that is transferred to the provincial governments, three provincial governments in this case, moneys that they use to spend to provide housing for the elderly in the case of a senior citizens' complex or a nursing home. At the end of every month the provincial government, which guarantees occupancy m those nursing homes and senior citizens' complexes, that are subsidized by the govern-

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
ment, sends in a bill to the federal government and the federal government pays a percentage of the cost.
This bill will reduce the amount of money. It will put a cap on the Canada Assistance Plan. It will put a cap on the CAP. Well, the cap on the CAP not only covers the senior citizens' complexes, but it covers every amount of money that is given out to people under what we call social assistance, and what some people refer to as welfare.
It caps the CAP in three provinces. Why does it do that? The hon. member for St. John's West is here now and he is saying: "Yes, it does this in three provinces".
The reason why this bill is being brought in, I believe, is because they have already put a cap on the other provinces. They have already put a cap on everything that can be capped. In other words, in the riding of the hon. member who interjected a few moments ago, in his province, the federal government has said this year: "We are going to reduce the amount of money that we transfer to your province. We are going to cap it at 3 per cent".
In other words, in the operations of a hospital or in the money for universities, they have been capped as well. To get at the other three provinces which are not given equalization payments, the government decided to cap the CAP. Now everyone is capped. In other words, the cost of running hospitals is capped, the administration of post-secondary institutions-our universities, trade colleges and vocational schools-is capped and now the social assistance departments are capped as well.
When their moneys are capped at 3 per cent or 5 per cent, it means that they cannot pay salary increases of 10 per cent, 7 per cent, 6 per cent or 5 per cent. They cannot buy new machinery and increase the costs of running hospitals.
The hon. member for the NDP made reference a few moments ago to medicare and a program by Walter Cronkite. I saw that particular program. It certainly was a sad hour to watch. There were people who had received two or three treatments of chemotherapy for cancer. They were left not being able to go back to the doctor or the hospital to receive further treatments of chemotherapy because the insurance company said: "Too bad, we are not going to insure you again unless you pay us $20,000 or $30,000."
It was a sad program to watch, and it was a sad reflection on how the United States of America takes care of some people who are caught in the bind of not having a system like we have in Canada.
In that program it gave the numbers on the most modem types of machinery that we have in our hospitals to take care of our sick. It gave examples of a machine like a CAT scan, and it gave the numbers for the United States as compared to Canada.
It was very clear that in the United States they were farther ahead of Canada with the machinery and the new modem methods of dealing with and detecting a disease than we in our hospitals.
I was thinking as I watched that program that we have many instances of that. We have our provincial administrations today and the federal government really costsharing to send a great many people to the United States for treatment on various types of machinery in hospitals that we do not have here in Canada, or that we do not have enough of.
I was dealing the other day with a case of somebody who needed the use of what is called a lithotripter machine. That is a machine that is available in Halifax, Nova Scotia, at the Victoria General Hospital. Of course, that is overworked so the provinces send patients either there or to another hospital to where that piece of machinery is.
How can a hospital or a provincial government buy all of that machinery and expand on its facilities when they have been capped by the federal government, when their amount of money has been reduced by the federal government?
The same thing applies to post-secondary education. Here, in this bill, we come to another bad case of reducing money to people who cannot afford to be caught.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, how difficult it is for somebody to live on social assistance today in this country? You can compare the amounts they receive for social assistance right across Canada and you discover that the amounts vary from province to province.
As a general rule, a single person would get about $120 a month to live on. If you are living at home, that varies $70 to $90. The provincial governments certainly cannot afford to cut back any more on those people who are on social assistance.
September 23, 1991

The federal government, along with these bills, turned around and discontinued the extent of our direct job creation programs.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, you cannot now get on a direct job creation program unless it is connected with the unemployment insurance fund. You have to be drawing unemployment insurance in order to get on to a works program.
What the provincial governments have done is come up with their own program to try to put people on unemployment insurance in order to save money through their social assistance grants and programs that they have available provincially.
The federal government has done this, as the hon. member said a few moments ago, in the name of attacking the national debt. We just dealt with a bill before this Chamber that imposed a 7 per cent tax called the GST and then established a special fund to retire the national debt. That argument presented by the Government of Canada to reduce the payments for social assistance across Canada does not apply today because it claims that now the new GST will do the job for it.
The federal government has even gone beyond capping amounts of money to provinces. Because of this bill passing through the House, three provincial governments will now have to pay money back to the federal Treasury, either in an outright cheque for millions and millions of dollars or they will have to do what the federal government has done with the province of Newfoundland for this year, and that is have the provinces pay back so much at the end of every two weeks.
In other words, for all of this year the province of Newfoundland is sending a cheque off to the federal Treasury to pay back what the federal Treasury claimed was an overpayment made to the province of Newfoundland over the last three or four years.
Perhaps we will see the same thing happen here. Not only are they being capped, not only are they being limited in the amount of money being transferred to them, but they have now been asked to pay back money that was granted to the provinces three, four and five years ago.
Government Orders
I think the federal government should have learned a lesson by now and admit that it cannot cut back in these areas. Of all the areas that could be listed to cut back in, you should never, ever touch health care, education and social assistance. Of the three areas, our hospitals and post-secondary institutions unfortunately have become places for only the well-to-do in our society, the very well-to-do.
The way our student loan system has been structured and now taxed by the Government of Canada, it is very difficult for somebody to go to university unless they have lots of money in the bank or parents who have lots of money to give to them. Now it is attacking not only our hospitals, our students, but the poorest of the poor, our senior citizens and their accommodations and our poor people who are on social assistance today and who cannot make ends meet.
The Government of Canada should hang its head in shame and withdraw this bill and pay to the people on social assistance what they need to keep their heads afloat with all of these new taxes we have circulating in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I did not realize that my good friend from Gander-Grand Falls would say so succinctly what he said so well.
However, if you will just give me a moment here, I will get organized.
I thank my friend, the distinguished former Speaker of this Chamber for the coaching. I need all the help I can get at this particular point, as I am sure he is aware.
As my friend from Gander-Grand Falls was saying when he was in full flight a few moments ago, this is just the latest attempt, not an isolated attempt but the latest of several attempts by this government to hoodwink a lot of people.
I recognize the government does not have great difficulty hoodwinking the member for South Shore. He has a vested interest in being hoodwinked.
He is hoodwinkable.

I am far more interested in the people who are being directly pounded into the ground by this particular piece of legislation. It sets about extending that cap on the Canada Assistance Plan.

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
The devastation that this government is wreaking on ordinary people across this country needs to be quantified if that is possible. If we could only bring before the House some specific examples of how people are being pummelled by this particular government.
Let me give just an example that I ran into this week. It is not under the ambit of the Canada Assistance Plan, but it is a parallel example that I believe will drive home the point that I want to make here.
I was in the home of an individual, a college student, this weekend in a small community on the south coast of Newfoundland, a community of about 200 or 300 people. This young woman is the daughter of a fisherman who had a fair to middling year, not a good year. He has caught some fish and he is still working but he has no great amount of income. Notwithstanding, when that young individual went to apply for a Canada student loan she was told that given her circumstances and those of her father and so on, she would qualify, not for the $900 or $1,000 which she wanted but for $155.
Point number one: the reason she is qualifying for such a measly amount is because this government has not changed the basic ground rules since 1984. It has not kept up with inflation over those past seven years. Whatever an amount was worth in 1984, it is certainly not worth the same amount seven years later given the effect of inflation. To begin with, it has not changed the ground rules. That is quite another story, an important one but another story. On to my example.
This young woman was informed that she qualified for $155 to help her through her year at college, $155. She is going to appeal that, and we will help her. In the meantime, she trots off to the local bank a few miles down the road to get her $155. As she is about to sign all the forms and to receive the $155, which is several hundred dollars less than she was hoping she would get, the bank people said to her: "There are a few more details. Before we can give you the $155 you owe us $4.65". She wanted to know what that was for. That was the tax. That is the 3 per cent tax, another of the several taxes this government has put on education. The goods and services tax is also a tax on education. There is a theme on which we could go for some time.
My friend from South Shore has a nice term for everything. People these days call janitors or whatever sanitary engineers. Is that right? He is the kind of individual who goes around inventing fancy terms to put a nice face on some pretty despicable stuff. He can call it what he wants, but I call it a kick in the guts for students. That is what I would call it. Instead of engaging in sweet phrasing, when is he going to start fighting for those students in his own riding who must be pummelled by those taxes?
Let me continue with the example. I am sure he would be interested. He looks at least amused by the example, so let me continue.
This young woman is asked for $4.65 before she can get her student loan. She was told it was a federal government tax on student loans. So she said: "Take it off the $155". "No, we cannot do that. The rules do not allow us to do that. You have to give us the $4.65 first and then we will give you the $155".
She searched around in her purse and scraped up $4.65 and she passed it across the counter.
The bank is not finished with her yet. There is one more wrinkle. It said: "Now that you have paid us the $4.65, we have got to send it to the government. So you have got to buy a money order to send the $4.65 to the government". She searched around in her purse some more and $1.50 later she has got her transaction completed. To get her $155 loan which is only a fraction, only one-sixth of what she needs in the first place, she has to pay a tax that the finance minister and the boys have dreamed up for $4.65. Then to get that tax into the hot little hands of the Minister of Finance, she has got to turn around and buy a money order, another $1.50.
What are we trying to do in this country? Are we trying to drive those young people stark raving mad before they ever get in the door the first time to further their education? I say to my friend in the NDP that the one thing that they will not make of those people are Tories. They are working on alienating those people completely. They are working on running them out of rural Newfoundland or rural Canada and in the process they make every waking moment just as miserable as they can.

Think of the example that I have given. To get $155, she pays $4.65 in federal tax, a student tax, a tax on education, and then she has to turn around and buy a money order to send the tax off to the government.
There must be people over there who sit up nights saying: "How can we make it even more miserable tomorrow than it is today for the ordinary people out there? How can we do something to aggravate them, to drive them clean up the wall, to drive them stark raving mad?" This bill, this cap on the Canada Assistance Plan, while not as dramatic as the example I just mentioned, is in the same vein. It is of the same ilk. It is crafted by a bunch of warped minds that are so out of touch with reality, the reality of life for people out there in Newfoundland, in rural Canada and all over this great country, once great country which is only a shadow of its former self, thanks to what the gentleman from Baie Comeau and his clique have done with it.
People all over this country are hurting. They are hurting and it chooses this time to bring in this kind of a bill, this kind of a double whammy, this kind of a kick in the guts.
I was going to say I do not understand what makes this crowd over there tick, but then I do. It is that philosophy, that right wing agenda that somehow says: "If through no fault of your own you don't have a job or if for reasons of personal or whatever kind of misfortune you don't have adequate access to income, enough to keep body and soul together, if you happen to be in that category, tough luck". It is called, kick them while they are down.
If we were to characterize the approach of this government toward poor people, toward the disadvantaged generally across this country, it is kick them while they are down. The thing that really boggles my mind and tears at everything that is in me is how otherwise decent men and women can sit over there and be the unwitting parrots to this kind of nonsense, this kind of cruelty. How can they be party to perpetrating on poor people across this country what this bill seeks to do and what this government seeks to do on a daily basis?
The only surprise is that this crowd is at 12 per cent in the polls, that it is that far up. That is the only surprise.

"Seventeen on Monday", the member for South Shore says. Enjoy it while it lasts. I say to him: enjoy it while it is up there at 17 per cent. It is a temporary situation if the people of this country continue to have the kind of basic horse sense that I know them to have. They will not stand by-
-another part of the horse.

I think the member is much too kind. The member for South Shore should get his seat moved so he can be a seatmate of the member for Burlington. He would make the member for Burlington look good. Now if that is his attempt at wit he is half way there.
Mr. Speaker, we are talking about what we can do under the aegis of the Canada Assistance Plan to help some of the ordinary people of Canada. The best that my friend from South Shore can do is sit here and dream up some more insults. He needs a few more lessons from the member for Burlington because the member for Burlington is light years behind him. But he is definitely going in the right direction and he should work on it-or, I should say, he should not work on it.
Mr. Speaker, who is going to benefit from this bill? I say the same people that the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs rushed out to call today, the Business Council on National Issues, his buddies in business. That is part of the right wing agenda; move away from the ordinary people every last nickel and dime you can, so that the well to do people in this country have ever-increasing amounts of disposable income. Do you know that if you were poor in 1984 when this government came to power and had an income of under $25,000, your taxes have gone up in the seven intervening years by $1,200. The member for South Shore is having trouble absorbing that, but that is not a surprise to me. He should check his facts. The advice he gave me-and I rushed out and I checked my facts and, as usual, he was absolutely right; the public debt in 1984 was not $170 billion, it was $167 billion. So I was off by a mere $3 billion. He now bids for $199 billion; do I hear $200 billion? Because whether we are talking $167 billion, $170 billion, or whether we are talking $199 or $200 billion, my point stands, that the debt now is over $400 billion and no amount of fiddling around with compound interest or double talk or insults will change that. The public debt since his administration took office has more than doubled. That is the point I was making to him. He skated beautifully.

He skated beautifully. Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attentiveness and care to my hon. friend from Burin-St. George's. I listened to
him talk about the people who are going to be disadvantaged by this legislation. It is interesting to observe that not a single Newfoundlander will be disadvantaged by this bill. It was interesting to note in my hon. friend's remarks that he said: "If the Tories do not stop taking money away from people there will not be any Tories left." One of the reasons this country is in such a mess is that the philosophy of the Liberal government was: "Buy as many of them as you can for as long as you can." The Liberals left office in 1984 with a $16 billion operating deficit.
If my hon. friend had come into office in 1984 and he was the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance all wrapped up into one and he inherited a $16 billion operating deficit and a $400 billion accumulated debt, what would his solution have been to this situation?

Mr. Speaker, the member in his last phrase or so unwittingly put a lie to everything he was saying. He should realize that the government which he supports inherited a debt of $167 billion. How many times do I have to say that to him? It was not $400 billion, it was $167 billion.
I heard the member say, Mr. Speaker, it was an inherited debt of $400 billion and it was actually $167 billion. Now he goes for $200 billion again. Do I hear $201 billion? In that example alone, it shows the member that if he is going to skate he should at least put the skates on. He should at least know how to do it.
The hon. member talks about inheriting an operating deficit of $16 billion. He is absolutely right, Mr. Speaker. speechtext: Order, please. On a point of order, the hon. member for South Shore.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know it is not my hon. friend's intention to mislead the House, but we have a $12.5 billion operating surplus today from a $16 billion operating deficit when his party left office.

I just want to continue with the answer to my colleague's question. He made the allegation that no Newfoundlander would be disenfranchised or hurt by this particular bill. Of course, he knows that is not the case at all. This is the old, foot-in-the-door approach. Today it happens to be Alberta, B.C. and Ontario. But once the government gets its foot in the door on this one, and does it with the unwitting support of people like the gentleman from South Shore, then tomorrow the world. Where will it stop? Where will it stop once it is allowed to make an onslaught on one of the programs that has served this country very well and helped look after the poor and the disadvantaged people of this country?
We cannot stand idly by and have these people doctor a very good program in the instance of shuffling a few more millions of dollars over to their rich buddies so they can make the tax break even greater for the people in the $100,000 bracket. That is our concern. It has to do with how you distribute income in this country.
If every decision was based on the bottom line we would not need a government at all. Those who have, have more and those who do not, shoot them. I do not subscribe to that philosophy, but this crowd does. I am not going to sit around and let them bulldoze their way through here with more policies that move this government's agenda further and further to the right. It is absolutely wrong and it belies the real reason we have government in the first place.
One of the reasons we have a government is to redistribute income to people who do not have income. That bill is a step in the wrong direction and I am going to oppose it for that reason.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague spoke very eloquently and quite extensively about the deficit and about the accumulated debt. I

would like him to make a few comments about what this bill is going to do to universality, particularly when we are talking about health care and education.
I would like to bring to the attention of my colleague the fact that by the year 2004, there will be no transfer payments from the federal government to the provinces in the areas of education and health care. How can the government have any say in those two areas if it does not make any financial contributions to the provinces?
I want him to tell Canadians, in his view, whether that will weaken the ability of the federal government in setting standards when it comes to health care and also when it was talking about national education objectives.
I want to hear a few comments from the hon. member on the impact of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my good friend from Ottawa Centre. He makes the points very well.
First, on the question of universality and what it is going to do to people across this country who need dental care and disabled people who need living services, foster homes for abused children, places for abused women, child care for low income families, all services provided through the Canada Assistance Plan are under threat.
The member for Ottawa Centre talks about one of the much touted phrases of this government. He talks about national educational objectives.
Well, I say through him to this House: What a joke. Here is a government which, when it writes throne speeches or budget speeches can get much exercised by national educational objectives. I am a former educator and there are many sitting in this Chamber. Who of us will not say that we have become too compartmentalized. We have different objectives and different standards in little pockets all across this country and that has to change if we are going to be competitive.
Do I sound like the former Minister of Finance? These were his words, but he has never put his money where his mouth is.

Now, with this bill and with other initiatives in this House, I say to my friend from Ottawa Centre, that former minister, the present Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and the rest of them over there are militating against our having national educational objectives. They are militating against our having a national standard of health care.
That is the real reason we on this side will fight this bill. It is a foot in the door that we do not want to go through.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to stand and to speak on this bill.
It is important that Canadians realize and know that the Canada Assistance Plan is the only way that the federal government transfers funds for the purposes of assisting in social assistance programs and social services. There is no other mechanism.
When we look at what this government is doing now, such as putting caps on this CAP, it is attacking our social programs. The Prime Minister said during his campaign debate that was a sacred trust. That is hypocrisy in the worst form. He campaigned strongly and clearly, saying: "This is a sacred trust. You have nothing to fear. The free trade agreement will not touch our social programs. You have my word on it."
So much for the Prime Minister's words, Mr. Speaker. The Canada Assistance Plan is being capped for the three richest provinces: Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, the three richest provinces, which have 50 per cent of the poor within their boundaries. That does not make a lot of sense to me.
How do you explain to those people who are the poorest in those three provinces who send their children to school hungry and with clothes that are full of holes and shoes that are perhaps not fully soled? How do you explain to them that they have nothing to fear, that they live in one of the richest provinces in Canada.
It does not take away the pains of hunger. It does not take away the humiliation of the parents who have to go and ask for this welfare assistance. No, Mr. Speaker, quite to the contrary.
What this government should be doing is trying to help people to get back on their feet and to become contributors once again to this society. This government has an obligation to look at job creation programs.
We look at what is going on today in the country and we see thousands and thousands of people losing their jobs every day. They go to the unemployment office and try to receive benefits from the unemployment office, and they are told: "You did not work enough. You do not have enough weeks to apply. We cannot help you. Go to the welfare office."
Those same people who perhaps on occasion are able to collect unemployment insurance find out that the collection period is shortened. They are told: "Sorry, go to the welfare office."
The federal government is passing on its responsibilities to the provinces. At the same time, we hear the Prime Minister saying things to the premier of Ontario like: "The welfare roles are going up." It is no surprise, because he is washing his hands of the needs of the people of Canada.
The Government of Ontario is not ready to sit back and watch people starve. It is that simple. It is one thing for this government to say: "We have to show restraint. We need to have fiscal restraint. We have to get our deficit under control." On whose back are they doing it? On the less fortunate, that is whose back they are doing it on. By cutting back on those social programs in the form of CAP reductions, they are doing it on the backs of the Canadians who can least afford it.
We heard talk about the G-7 nations, the Group of Seven. There are a couple of notes I would like to read into the record just so that people understand a little more of what G-7 is all about. The G-7 is made up of the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada. Of the G-7 Canada has by far the highest percentage of total taxes paid from personal income, which leads me to the point of corporate tax. We hear people say that the NDPers are always talking about taxing corporations, always talking about passing the buck on to the corporations. It is not fair. Let us have a minimum tax for corporations.
We are then told that if you keep doing that the corporations are going to move to the United States. Let me remind you, my friends, that the United States has a minimum corporate tax of 20 per cent.

If we had a minimum corporate tax of 20 per cent here in this country, we could raise some $8 billion through that minimum tax.
Are we going to scare people away by saying we are going to have a minimum corporate tax? I do not think so because we see more and more that the manufacturers are leaving the country as it is. Why are they leaving the country now? We do not have a minimum tax. Why are they leaving? Why are we having so much unemployment in this country? It is because of the high dollar, the high interest rate policy that we have.
I would like to return for a moment to the social assistance program as we know it today. It is set up not to be a way for people to establish a lifestyle. Our social assistance program is a temporary measure to assist people when the need is greatest. It should not be institutionalized. We should not look to institutionalized food banks. We should try to find ways of getting people back to gainful employment.
That is the thrust of the message I am trying to get across here today. People in Canada are proud. They do not want a program of assistance to which they can adjust themselves to so that they can live free. No one in this country should get a free ride. Everybody has to contribute in one way or another.
I think that what this government should be looking at are more creative ways of creating jobs, of getting people back to work. I think that is going to be the solution to our problems in this country.
I have to restate that the burden of responsibility belongs on the shoulders of the federal government to assist the provinces in the continuation of these programs to aid those people who need it the most. Its corporate friends are not the ones who need it the most. The loopholes have to be closed in order to raise the funds that are needed to continue funding these programs. The federal government cannot pass its burden of responsibility to the provinces which in turn have no choice but to pass it on to the municipalities because that is where the welfare comes from, the ranks of the municipal taxpayers.
At the bottom line, I have heard people ask who pays. Sure it is the taxpayers who pay, but when you are taking 10 jelly beans out of a pot that has 15, or taking 10 jelly beans out of a pot that has 15 million, which one will you
Government Orders
notice the most? If you are taking from the bigger pot, the effect is felt by fewer people. That is exactly what I am saying about this government. When we are drawing from the federal pot, everyone contributes and the effects are felt less strongly than they would be if they were taken from the municipal and the provincial pot.
Clearly, this federal government has missed the target altogether.
The federal government has said that it would like to eliminate child poverty by the year 2000. Is this its response? Is this the way it is going to do it? You cannot keep taking away and taking away and expect people to continue to survive.
I believe we need some restructuring. We have to look at our tax structure to ensure that we all pay our fair share. No one in this country would object to paying their fair share. But the imbalance we have today is a bloody nightmare. There are people paying 7 per cent who are making millions. There are people who are paying 35 per cent who are making peanuts. There is a severe imbalance.
We have to look at our training programs so that people can adjust themselves to the technological change we see taking place in the country today. People on unemployment insurance are running out of benefits and are not receiving training. I get any number of calls in my office from people telling me that they have an opportunity for a job. They have gone to the Canada Employment Centre and asked for some training to do this job, only to be told that it does not fall within the parameters of the training program being offered by that office.
I had one incident where a person came to me and said: "I have a job driving heavy equipment. I need two months training. The employer gave me a letter telling me that I have the job". He showed me the letter. "I have the job and I need two months training, but he will not pay for the training. If I can get the training through UI, through the Canada Employment Centre, I have the job".
He went to the UI and he was told: "Sorry, that does not fall within the parameters of our retraining program". He did not get the job.

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
There are instances where the system is inflexible and it will not adapt itself to the needs of the people. We have a system where we have to adjust to the system.
When we look at single industry towns where there is limited opportunity for employment, what is this government doing to diversify that economy? What is it doing?
FEDNOR is an excellent program. I have no shame and no hesitation in commending the government when I agree with a program it has. FEDNOR is one of those programs. I have told the minister that it needs some flexibility, that it needs a broadening of the base and needs some changes. I wrote him a letter and as far as I know, he agrees and it is something that is being looked at.
A the same time, when we look at the retraining program through the UI, that is a whole different picture. "Sorry, that is not what we are looking at. That is not what we want to do. That does not fit within the parameters of the mandate". Well, what are the parameters of the mandate? What is it we want to do? We want to put people back to work. We want to get them off the social assistance programs. People in this country want to work. They do not want social benefits. But by God, if they need them they should be there. They should not be told: "I am sorry, but the pot is empty. So you go hungry. You do not meet the guidelines. You go without". That is not what this is all about. There is approximately $1.6 billion going to the Ontario government in Canada Assistance Plan money. That is an indication that there is a severe need for a restructuring of training, of where we are going. Is it the intent that we become a welfare state? It seems to me that that is where we are headed. More and more people are out of work and less and less is being done to help put them back to work.
Statistically, if my information is correct-and I have no reason to doubt that it is-if you take a person out of the work force for a period of two years, you have a very slim chance of getting that person back into the work force. That person will at that point have adjusted himself or herself to a system of social assistance where they have changed their lifestyle. They have learned to do without. They have learned to cut back. They have learned to tell their children: "I am sorry, you just cannot go to the show this month. Maybe in a couple of months we will save enough money that you can go to the show". They have adjusted themselves to that kind of a program.
That is not acceptable to me. That is not acceptable to any Canadian. Canadians want to work.
When we look at the whole question of CAP, at social assistance benefits, safe houses for battered women, the children's aid societies, when we look at any other government funded agencies that are funded through the Canada Assistance Plan, that is funded by the federal government in which that is the only way the federal government participates, I cannot accept, I will not accept that this government should be allowed to put a cap on it.
If the need is there, the funds should be there to assist on a temporary basis and, more important, we should be looking toward a better job creation program so that these people can become proud once again and contribute in the way they want to contribute to the economy in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend a couple of questions. Ele has tried in his speech to point to new sources of income for looking after those disadvantaged in our society. I appreciate the importance of the subject.
I want to question him on the two proposals he had which were pretty substantive. The first was the suggestion that we get rid of all loopholes in the Income Tax Act so that we can produce more revenue to look after the lower income people in Canada. We have, as the hon. member knows, since 1984 pruned from the Income Tax Act just about every loophole that the Liberals have put in there.
The scientific research tax credit was the worst. Almost $2 billion had been siphoned out of the taxpayers' hands through that scheme. The last one that we got rid of was the flow-through shares scheme which was important for the mining industry. What would he say? Does he support the removal of flow-through shares because that is a loophole which we did remove?
My second question has to do with taxing corporations, having a minimum tax on corporations. We have in Canada now over one million taxable corporations. A large number of them are sub-companies of larger holding groups. Therefore if you tax them, you would be taxing them once as the entity itself and once as the holding company. Is he in favour of taxing twice?

The second group of corporations that are not taxed are corporations that have loss carry-forwards. They have lost a whole bunch of money for two or three years, and they finally make a profit. They put the past years' losses against the profits and they are not taxable. Does the hon. member want to tax companies with loss carry-forwards?
In the third group we have over 800,000 companies in Canada with sales of less than $200,000. Is that who he wants to tax? There are not really very many companies left that do not pay tax, that really are worthy payers of tax in my view, so I would like his answers to those two questions.

I would like to thank the hon. minister for his question because I think they are veiy important.
First of all on flow-through shares, as the minister very well knows the original flow-through share program as we knew it was severely flawed and there was severe abuse.
The second Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program, CEDIP, was also somewhat flawed but a little less than the flow-through shares.
No, I would rather support quite clearly what industry is asking for now which is an adjustment to the cost price of a flow-through share. That would then give them money to continue exploration and create jobs.

I have never said I was opposed to assisting companies, corporations, call them whatever you like, that want to create or continue and expand employment.
If the loophole does nothing more than take the money and put it in their pocket and walk away, I am sorry I do not support that, and I do not think the minister does either.
What I am saying is that if we are going to create employment, if we are going to ensure the continuation of employment, then there definitely should be some assistance, but not if it is only to put money in their pockets.
On the question of double taxing of corporations, clearly a fair taxation system is what I have always

wanted and what the New Democratic Party has always wanted, fairness and equality. Thx profitable corporations. If they do not make a profit clearly you are not going to tax them. That would not be fair. I do not think anyone in our party has ever said to tax companies that are going broke or to tax people who are closing shop or to tax people who are trying to create some employment but are having some difficulty. We never said that. I do not think anyone here has ever said that. I certainly have not.
When I made my comment about raising $8 billion in additional taxes, when I mentioned the 20 per cent minimum corporate tax, I was quoting from memory but I have the article here from The Financial Post in January 1990. They said: "$8.2 billion in additional revenue could have been raised in 1987, if a minimum corporate tax of 20 per cent had been in effect". This is for all profitable corporations.
I think I have addressed the questions of the minister and the evidence is there.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to ask a question of the member for Timmins. With regard to what is happening with the capping and so on, does the member agree with the proposal that has been put forward by Premier Bob Rae of Ontario to bring in a social charter that all governments in the future would have to recognize? Does he see that there is a need for social programs in Canada, particularly when we see food banks at the extent they are, when we see governments cutting back in social programs in the very areas they are needed most? Possibly at this time, when a constitution is being debated, it is time for a social charter to be adopted across Canada to identify those problems and ensure that they are looked after by all governments.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question. I certainly do agree with Premier Bob Rae of Ontario. We have to ensure that when the need is there-and let us be honest that it will probably always be there- the program that is required to assist these people is there as well. We have to ensure there is some kind of protection for these people when social assistance is required and that they do not have to get down on their knees and go begging hat in hand. We have to ensure that they are protected and that the children in particular are protected.

Government Orders
I applaud Premier Bob Rae for his initiative. I certainly hope that he will get the support of all the premiers and of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I am busy on my feet today because there is a lot to be said about the government's economic fiscal and legislative program that it has put in place.
Earlier today I talked about the inequity in the government's approach to wage parity. I think this particular bill, Bill C-32, is another example of how this government has lost absolute control over its own agenda.
I remember just a very few years ago when I was running in my first election campaign federally in 1988. Goodness knows and God forbid, it sounded like if you elected a Conservative government again there was not going to be one chicken in every pot but there was going to be two chickens in every pot and a bigger car in every driveway.
I specifically remember the former Minister of Finance indicating clearly that the deficit was under control, the economy was under an expansion period, and saying "just elect us one more time and we are going to give you everything you ever dreamed of".
The people of Canada may have got sucked in back in 1988, but it is pieces of legislation like this, Bill C-32, that will ensure, as my hon. colleague from Newfoundland said, that Tories are going to be an endangered species after the next election.
What this government clearly has done is to dismantle the social system, the social network, that social net that we have built in this country over generations. We have always believed that this was a country, even with crazy geography and even with the inequities that we see in this country, rich enough that government had a role to play in ensuring that it did not matter where you lived, it did not matter how rich or poor you were, that you had a right to expect certain things and certain standards and programs.
This government has completely abandoned the promises of its 1988 campaign, promises of prosperity. Lots of prosperity has happened. I checked with Reverend Chang in my constituency, a minister who is very active in trying to help those who need that extra special hand in times of need, the poorest of the poor. Lie tells that he
does not know what has happened, but for some strange reason that economic miracle has not hit some of the people in my riding or the people in ridings in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and all of the Atlantic, because we have never seen as many hungry people going to food banks. We have never seen so many people cut off from the economic greatness of this country. We have never seen church basements with so many people lined up looking for food for their children.
Where is the prosperity? What kind of an economic agenda has this government followed?
Let us look at it. Back in 1988 we were told that another term of Toryism, another term with these people opposite in power, was going to change the country. Brian Mulroney said it best: "Give me four more years and you will not even know this country".
There are a lot of people in this country who would like to go back about seven years because what this Prime Minister and this government have done has been nothing short of disastrous and an abuse of the public trust that was put into this government. Prosperity is not bursting out all over. Poverty, dismay and disunity have been the legacy of this government.
We have Bill C-32. This bill talks about fairness. It says, sorry, but the poorest of the poor, those people who want a job, who want to contribute, who want their children to feel that they belong and who do not want to be on welfare, are the people who are going to have to bear the burden more than anyone else in this country of this government's economic mismanagement, of its foolhardy policies.
There was a member opposite, the member for South Shore, who would have done well to sit down because I hope his constituents heard what he had to say on this particular issue. Maybe Nova Scotia is not affected, but this is the thin edge of the wedge. Give these guys across the aisle an inch and they will take a mile.
I remember the former minister for ACOA from Central Nova Scotia. He was out there beating the bushes telling us how great things were going to be in Nova Scotia because this government was committed, sacred trust, to regional development. We certainly found out what that sacred trust did. That sacred trust saw in the first two years of this government, $1.14
September 23, 1991

billion-that is a lot of money-cut from regional development programs in Atlantic Canada.
What effect do you think that has? I guess this government thinks it has no effect. It has a large effect because the unemployment rates went up. We became less competitive in the fisheries. We have seen our manufacturing base decline. This government calls that a continuing commitment to regional development.
We have also seen this government, as it tries to inflict prosperity from coast to coast in this country, come up and establish program financing.
Do you remember the principle this country was based on? It was caring and sharing. We said we have this program, it is called Established Programs Financing, and that is put there to ensure that it does not matter if you are in a province like Newfoundland, which is having some economic difficulties right now, or Nova Scotia, or if you are in Alberta where things are in fairly good shape or were before this government got in power. EPF ensured that there were transfers to those provinces for health care and post-secondary education. That is pretty important. If I cannot feel like a first-class Canadian in any province, and know that I have access to first-class health care and first-class post-secondary education, then there is something wrong with this country. It has pulled a thread out of this country which has damaged the fabric forever.
Let us look at Established Programs Financing. What has it done with it? I am going to quote right here from a brief that was given to a committee of Parliament studying bankruptcy legislation. It is from the Canadian Hospital Association.
The Canadian Hospital Association says that the changes in the EPF formula that this government has done in three successive budgets have the following effects. The transfer of responsibility to some of Canada's poorest provinces as a result of the changes to the EPF are as follows: between 1986 and 199, this government is cutting from transfers to the provinces for health care over $29 billion, $29,998 billion. That might be okay if you are in a province that has not been devastated by a recession or this government's policies. It is not okay in those provinces that do not have that type of economic base. It means that either they are going to have to cut somewhere else where they cannot afford it or we are going to have two classes of Canadians: those who live in have provinces and can expect to get national standards
Government Orders
on programs, and those who live in have not provinces. Adios amigo, too bad, move to Toronto if you want to get a good bed and a good hospital.
Concerning post-secondary education, in a 10-year period between 1986 and 1996 it has cut $12,109 billion from those cost shared programs.
I heard the Prime Minister one day, I think it was during an election campaign, by God, saying that these things were sacred trusts. He even used his mother as a prop for goodness' sake to tell the Canadian public he would not touch any of these things. My goodness, it was those dastardly old Liberals and NDP members when they were going out and saying elect this bunch again and your social programs are going to be gone.
The government ensured that it once again was able to fool the Canadian public, and now we have seen two and a half years of Tory policies dismantle the social safety net in this country.
If that was not bad enough, a year ago, I think it was in April 1990, this government's spending was out of control. It was collecting more in taxes than any other government ever had. I think at that point it had raised taxes over 30 times. The money was coming in hand over fist. These guys opposite were spending it faster than it was coming in. They had taxed the Canadian public to the limit.
If that was not enough, they then decided that they were going to change the way the equalization formula works. There was some obscure clause that would kick in at a certain point, but they did not bother to tell the provinces about it.
The result in April 1990 was that Canada's smallest province and one of its poorest provinces, Prince Edward Island, suddenly found itself when the Minister of Finance was about to put a budget down $13 million short.
I think $13 million in a big province is a lot of money. Put it in a province with 135,000 people and it is absolutely devastating.
Then just three weeks later the province of Nova Scotia, again a have not province, found out that because the government and the bright boys and girls at the Department of Finance figured out another way to squeeze the poorest provinces it was going to lose $65 million in its provincial budget.

September 23, 1991
Government Orders
It is okay to say: "We have to share the burden here". If we are going to share the burden, why in the name of goodness do we not get to share the benefit when there are good times? We do not do that in places like Atlantic Canada.
This government comes in with its triple play, Bill C-32, the cap on CAP. If this government is allowed to go unchecked, it will not only ruin the economy but it will create a checkerboard Canada.
If you happen to live in a relatively prosperous region you can expect certain things. If you do not then you can expect not to have those certain things. Bill C-32, more than any other bill that has come before this place, is a glaring example of how this government has broken its social contract.
It is okay to say: "Ontario, you are kind of wealthy. Alberta, you are kind of wealthy. Maybe right now we are going to cap you". The problem is that the growing number of those who are unemployed and the growing number of those who find themselves in poverty are not capped. They increase every single day.
We are becoming more like Americans. We are trying to put a system in place here that rewards success. It absolutely throws those people who slip from the ladder of success into the trash heap. That is absolutely against every single thing that the Liberal Party tried to do in government and in forging a social contract with people of this country.
These Tories opposite sit back. With their smugness they say: "That is too bad. Let the poor people out there get jobs". That is the type of response you will get from some people opposite.
The fact is that the government has taken in more revenue than any other government. It has transferred the debt to the provinces. It has not given the provinces the capability for additional taxation because it has milked the public dry.
It has put away half a million jobs.

It has put away half a million jobs.
We have had a free trade deal. Remember the wonderful free trade deal. The government opposite made it quite clear during free trade that it was going to be the panacea of everybody. There are going to be jobs flowing like milk and honey.
Just on the outside chance that there might be a job lost-you remember-it was going to have the most generous assistance program that the western world had ever seen. The minister walks behind me and says: "Yes". I hope he had a smile on his face and both fingers crossed, because he knows as well as every worker who has lost a job and an investment in their future and that of their family because of the free trade deal that it was simply not true.
This government's kamikaze economic policies have done more to separate us, to divide us, to categorize us and eventually, probably, to destroy this nation.
Bill C-32, as I said earlier, is the thin edge of the wedge. Today, maybe it applies to those provinces that this government in its warped sense of fairness feels can afford it.
Tomorrow, to my friend from Newfoundland who just spoke, it may apply to Newfoundland. The next day maybe it will apply to Saskatchewan or to British Columbia.
At some point, the federal government will absolutely shed like the skin of a lizard its responsibility to maintain those standards and that social contract with Canadians.
Even more important, what it is doing in places like Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan is making those governments pay dearly for the consequences of the actions of this government.
Jobs are going, half a million jobs. It will be a million jobs by the time these guys are finished. The poor are lining up at food banks. It does not get any better. It is the dismantling of Canada, as my friend from Ontario says. It is the dismantling of Canada.
Bill C-32, as I said earlier I think is going to go down as one of the most glaring examples. I cannot wait until we get on the campaign trail, because Bill C-32 is going to drive this government, not to its knees at 17 per cent; it will drive them into the Smithsonian Institute, the Museum of Civilization across from here. Because after the next election Bill C-32 is going to be indicative of the decline and fall of the Tory empire.
